item.title: Clocks, Barnacles, Ballots
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope you're doing well. Today, Thursday, October 29th, we'll look forward, backward, and through some stuff, so I'll get to it.
item.content:encoded:
I hope you're doing well. Today, Thursday, October 29th, we'll look forward, backward, and through some stuff, so I'll get to it.

First, early voting sites are open until 4 PM. If what's holding you back from voting is not knowing the who, what, when, where, and why, go to bkcb6.app/electionexplainer. After polls close, the Barnacle Parade kicks off at 4 in Coffey Park, and the Cobble Hill Health Center will be temporarily haunted. More matters of that ilk, including 3 parades, are listed at bkcb6.app/spooky.

Then, as spooky season officially ends and November begins, clocks go backward, voting ends, and thousands run through the CB6 and the city at large. A less alarmist way to put it is that on Sunday, November 1st, daylight saving time and early voting end, and the New York City Marathon will be held on a route that includes 4th Avenue. For more marathon information, like a layered map, visit bkcb6.app/marathon.

Third, beyond concerns of the following few days, I've compiled, and continue to compile, decades of data on housing costs and availability at bkcb6.app/housecostavail. One part of it is taking every listing from StreetEasy since 2010 in CB6, Brooklyn, and across NYC. You'll find out when you can expect to pay less than 2K a month in any CB6 neighborhood, but I won't spoil it. It also lists affordable (less expensive?) housing lotteries that are open, along with other options. This work focuses on availability and options, and on what it would take to move to CB6, or live elsewhere in the city at different points in time. It's here, in the app, and interactive. I'd say it's a good idea to follow up by taking our district needs survey.

With that, I'll close by suggesting you scroll and read the rest, whether you do or don't, and whether you've downloaded any apps. I wish you well.

item.title: Choices, Stickers, Plans
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope your week is off to a good start. I’ll start in our immediate orbit and go from there. Last night, our Business Affairs & Licensing Committee approved three liquor licenses, which now move…
item.content:encoded:
I hope your week is off to a good start. I’ll start in our immediate orbit and go from there. Last night, our Business Affairs & Licensing Committee approved three liquor licenses, which now move to the Full Board on Wednesday, November 18. One application was for a new Mexican restaurant in Carroll Gardens on Court St btwn 3rd & 4th Pl. The other 2 involve legal and ownership changes but remain the same restaurants: Piccoli Trattoria in Park Slope on 6th Ave & 14th St and, at the corner of Beard Street, Lundy’s in Red Hook.

Speaking of Red Hook, the 14th annual Barnacle Parade is Thursday at 4:00 PM, starting at Coffey Park to celebrate the neighborhood’s resilience on the anniversary of Hurricane Sandy. Most weeks, if there’s one parade, it's the only parade, but this week is built different. Which is to say we’ve actually got three more parades on Halloween: Cobble Hill’s at 4:00 PM, the Pirates of the Gowanus on the canal at 5:30 PM, and Park Slope’s on 14th Street at 6:30 PM. All of them, plus more Halloween events, trick-or-treat streets, and scary movie listings, are at bkcb6.app/spookycb6.

Between, before, and even a bit after any of those events, you can vote in this year's election; polls are open until 8 PM today. Personally, I vote early based on the stickers they hand out, so I’m debating whether to go on Saturday for a Halloween sticker or on Sunday for the newly minted marathon vote sticker. If you're unsure about the who, what, why, when, and where of voting, bkcb6.app/elections has got you covered. I even have some CB6 “I Voted” stickers I’m happy to part with if that’s of concern.

After hard-selling voting, I don’t want to risk choice fatigue, but I am going to say you should take our district needs and budget survey. You can jump right in and take the survey, or read about related matters here or in the app(s). Either way, it’ll register.

I won’t type much more, but I will recommend you read the rest, download, and enjoy the rest of your day whether you do anything mentioned or not.

item.title: Policy, Participating, Parades
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well after a week that included a committee meeting with crashcount.nyc and the Friends of Fort Defiance, and ahead of a weekend that kicks off early voting in this…
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well after a week that included a committee meeting with crashcount.nyc and the Friends of Fort Defiance, and ahead of a weekend that kicks off early voting in this year's general election.

A general election in which everyone's ballot will include Governor, Attorney General, Comptroller, and five possible City Charter changes. You'll also be able to vote for Congress, State Senate, State Assembly, and judges. If that piques your interest, go to our elections page, where, depending on your address, you'll find a sample ballot that tells you who, what, when, and where to vote.

The winners of those elections will have more than the advisory role I'm more familiar with in public policy matters. Election winners like Comptroller Levine and Borough President Reynoso focused on transportation policy in a recent letter to DOT, supporting and citing CB6 among the boards that have called for lowering speed limits under Sammy's Law and daylighting at street corners. You can see what both would mean for your block here. Another transportation policy is the proposed Bergen and Dean bike boulevard, which runs through four community boards and six council districts. If you're interested, DOT will hold two virtual workshops on Tuesday, November 10th, and Thursday, November 12th, both at 6:30 PM. You can register here, and what we know so far is here (& in the app!).

Housing policy is another area where policy election winners will have a say. For example, Block by Block, Mayor Mamdani's housing plan for 120 city-owned sites, or HPD's Fair Housing Growth Strategy, which former CB6 Land Use expert Rebecca Kobert helped develop and lays out a 2030 housing target for every district, including good ol CB6.

Housing and transportation have long been among our top concerns. If you'd like to tell us what yours are, take our District Needs Survey.

While not a traditional matter of public policy, thank you to everyone who volunteered to test the Android version of the apps, as we've more than tripled the required amount. So someday soon iPhone and Android alike will be able to download BKCB6, BKCB, or CBNYC.

Another non-policy policy is to stop typing here, recommend reading the rest, and wish you the best.

item.title: Meetings, Droids & More
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Hopefully, your week has gone well. I have a few things to share today.
item.content:encoded:
Hopefully, your week has gone well. I have a few things to share today.

First, thank you to everyone who has downloaded BKCB6 (almost a thousand so far). As I mentioned last week, it's the city's first community board app, and outside the central City government, it's also the only city government entity with one.

Second, today may not be a lucky day, but it is the day I received Google Play's approval. After 14 days of testing, the app will be on the Google Play Store for all. So if you're one of the folks who reached out, or even if you're not but use an Android device and want to test it, let me know. Basically, you can download the app now and tell me what you like, what you don't, and anything else you think.

Third, tonight, Wednesday, October 21st, at 6:30 PM, our Transportation, Parks and Transportation, Parks and Public Safety Committee will hear two presentations. One is from the creator of crashcount.nyc, and the other is from the Friends of Fort Defiance. The meeting will be held in person at Principles, 139 9th Street, and virtually over Zoom.

Fourth, tomorrow's Landmarks Committee meeting is canceled. On Monday, October 26th, at 6:30 PM, our Business Affairs and Licenses Committee will meet at 250 Baltic Street to review liquor license applications. The meeting may feel a bit less bookish than usual, as the library has started moving its materials back to the Carroll Gardens Library ahead of a December 1st reopening. Our next Full Board meeting will be on Wednesday, November 18th, since our usual meeting day would have fallen on Veterans Day.

Fifth, early voting for this year's general election starts this Saturday, October 24th. If you need to know where to vote and what's on your ballot, head to bkcb6.app/poll-finder-bk. App havers, of course, already have all of this in their pocket.

I'll stop here and suggest you scroll, download, and read the rest, but even if you stop here, I wish you the best.

item.title: First CB App, Not Last
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Brooklyn Community Board 6 is the first community board in New York City with its own app.
item.content:encoded:
Brooklyn Community Board 6 is the first community board in New York City with its own app.

It's called BKCB6, and it's free on the App Store(Android is on its way). We also have BKCB, the same idea for all 18 Brooklyn community boards, and CBNYC, which covers all 59 community boards in the five boroughs.

But for this newsletter, I'll focus on BKCB6.

The app puts everything in one place, hopefully in a way that's easier to understand and share. It's not set in stone, so I'm happy to make changes over time. While I don't know much about art in general, or cubism specifically, I remember a quote I always liked from a sculptor who compared cubism to standing on a mountain and looking around. Go higher or lower and things look different. "It is a point of view."

And that's what this hopes to be, a point of view.

Type in any address and you'll see the day's parking and trash pickup, the poll site, who represents it, the sample ballot, and any street work, film shoots, or block parties coming up in the next month. You can also look up 311 complaints, crime, parking tickets, and permits for any address or block, updated daily.

You'll also find every CB6 meeting and every set of minutes back to 2010 (and today's!). The calendar goes well beyond the board so that you can find things like the next Gowanus BID formation meeting or the 76th Precinct Community Council's schedule. Every lot in the district is mapped with its zoning and land use, along with the Gowanus rezoning and the BQE. The app also explains how the processes work: ULURP, the BSA, SEQR, and what you can build where.

Interactive versions of major plans, including the Brooklyn Comprehensive Plan, the Gowanus Rezoning, Mayor Mamdani's Block by Block plan, and the City's Fair Housing Growth Strategy, are also available.

A directory covers nearly 2,900 local businesses, the community groups, and every school, library, and park. It also has a Jobs tab with openings from SBIDC, New York City, and New York State. Most of it works offline, and it collects no data about you.

Download BKCB6 on the App Store. If you have any thoughts, let me know.

Related tools

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Block by Block, Site by Site
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Fifth tool, and the one that started this series: bkcb6.app/blockbyblock. Mayor Mamdani’s housing plan, Block by Block, mapped by community board and council district, with the Land Inventory Fast Track list at the center of it: all 120…
item.content:encoded:
Fifth tool, and the one that started this series: bkcb6.app/blockbyblock. Mayor Mamdani’s housing plan, Block by Block, mapped by community board and council district, with the Land Inventory Fast Track list at the center of it: all 120 city-owned sites, sortable by site, address, agency, neighborhood, council district, or community board, with a CB6-only view. Two are here, Gowanus Green and the Brooklyn Marine Terminal.

Alongside the list is the record it should be measured against: what each district built over the last ten years, how rents moved, and what got rezoned. For CB6 that includes Pratt’s Middle Housing Gone Missing, Rebecca Kobert’s study of neighborhood change in this district from 2003 to 2024, and our own district needs statement, where building and preserving housing is the top priority. The plan’s own words are on the page too, from chapter 4.2: the comprehensive 1961 rezoning reduced citywide housing capacity by 80 percent, and the regulatory tools that followed have frequently been used for exclusionary ends, especially in the city’s wealthiest, resource-rich neighborhoods.

A list of 120 is a list that can be 121. We’ve asked for 250 Baltic Street to be next.

Open Block by Block → · The Use of Land Hub

item.title: Land Use, Mapped
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Third tool: bkcb6.app/landusemap. Every lot in the city, colored three ways.
item.content:encoded:
Third tool: bkcb6.app/landusemap. Every lot in the city, colored three ways. Land use is what’s actually there: one- and two-family homes, walk-ups, elevator buildings, commercial, industrial, parks. Zoning is what the code allows there. Use groups is the finer grain of the zoning, the categories that decide whether a storefront can be a bar, a clinic, or a warehouse.

You can look at it by community board, by council district, by neighborhood, by borough, or the whole city at once. Set it to zoning and community boards and you can see, in one screen, why CB6 looks the way it does: the manufacturing zones along the canal and the waterfront, the low-rise residential blocks behind them, and the commercial corridors stitched through.

When a rezoning or a variance comes to the board, this is the map I’m looking at. Now it’s the map you can look at too.

Open the Land use map → · The Use of Land Hub

Best,

item.title: Gowanus, Explained
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Zoning determines what can legally be built on a piece of land. A rezoning changes what is and isn’t allowed.
item.content:encoded:
Zoning determines what can legally be built on a piece of land. A rezoning changes what is and isn’t allowed. In New York City that means the Uniform Land Use Review Procedure, ULURP, and in the case of Gowanus the applicant was the city itself. The result changed more than 80 blocks that were mostly industrial into a mixed-use district with over 9,000 units of housing, around 3,000 of them permanently affordable, more than six acres of new open space, and space for artists and industry.

Fourth tool in the Use of Land Hub: bkcb6.app/gowanus. It has a readable guide to the Special Gowanus Mixed Use District, Chapter 9 of the zoning resolution, with the full chapter one click away. It has the timeline from the first hearings through the Borough President’s approval and the Council vote in 2021. It sets CB6’s resolution side by side with the Points of Agreement signed by Mayor de Blasio and negotiated by Council Members Brad Lander and Stephen Levin, including the NYCHA capital investment, and it tracks the Gowanus Oversight Task Force that is supposed to hold everyone to them. Maps show land use, zoning districts, NYCHA sites, and current and future permits, so you can watch it get built.

If you want to understand the biggest change to this district in a generation, or hold people to what was promised, start here.

Open the Gowanus rezoning page → · The Use of Land Hub

item.title: The Use of Land
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: The use of land (more commonly land use, but I’m hoping you notice) is about who gets what, when, and how. What can be built, where, at what scale, and for whom is settled years before anything goes up, in applications most people never…
item.content:encoded:
The use of land (more commonly land use, but I’m hoping you notice) is about who gets what, when, and how. What can be built, where, at what scale, and for whom is settled years before anything goes up, in applications most people never see.

So I put everything I’ve built for reading that record in one place: bkcb6.app/useofland. Twenty tools, all public data, covering 59 community districts, 51 council districts and 388 neighborhoods.

A few of them: Block by block, the Mayor’s housing plan read against ten years of district data. Rents, every StreetEasy listing since 2010; play the timeline and watch rent move month by month by neighborhood, board, council district or borough. Land use map, every lot in the city shaded by land use or zoning. Less expensive housing, what you may qualify for by household and income, every open lottery, and Mitchell-Lama. NYS DHCR & Neighborhood Preservation, free housing help near you and where State housing money went. NYCHA, every development in the city, with the four in CB6. Plus the Brooklyn Marine Terminal, the Gowanus rezoning, what R, C and M actually allow at any address, every Landmarks application, all 70,832 homes in CB6 across 13,755 lots, who owns what, everything built since 2010, and every ULURP.

Why bother? Advising on policy well means starting from what is actually there. Our Statement of District Needs opens every year on the same premise: budgets are moral documents, and politics is who gets what, when, and how. Building and preserving housing has been our top priority year over year. The Mayor’s Block by Block plan lines up with what this board has been saying for a long time, and you can’t argue for adding to a list if you can’t read the list.

I’ll be adding to it, but let me know what you think. Also, if anyone is a non-iPhone user who would be interested in demoing the app so that it can be in the Google Play Store, let me know.

The Use of Land Hub →

item.title: Rents, Then and Now
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: The second tool in the Use of Land Hub is the one people ask me about most: bkcb6.app/rents. It maps median asking rents for every community board in the city, by unit size, month by month since January 2010, and lets you drag a slider…
item.content:encoded:
The second tool in the Use of Land Hub is the one people ask me about most: bkcb6.app/rents. It maps median asking rents for every community board in the city, by unit size, month by month since January 2010, and lets you drag a slider through sixteen years of it.

For CB6 the current picture is stark. A one-bedroom in Red Hook now lists around $4,395, Carroll Gardens $4,300, Gowanus $4,183, Park Slope $3,900, and Cobble Hill and the Columbia Street Waterfront around $3,200. Citywide, Brooklyn CB1 (Greenpoint and Williamsburg) sits at the top near $4,895 and CB16 (Brownsville) at the bottom near $1,500. CB6 has been in the highest band for most of the last decade.

The point of the tool isn’t to make anyone feel worse. It’s to put the same numbers in front of everyone before a hearing, a rezoning, or a budget vote, so the conversation starts from what rents actually are rather than what someone remembers paying. Pick a period, pick an area, generate the report, and bring it with you.

Open Rents → · The Use of Land Hub

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: Block, Baltic, Beyond
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: In May, Mayor Mamdani and Deputy Mayor Bozorg put out Block by Block, the administration’s housing plan. The part that matters most for us is the LIFT list, short for Land Inventory Fast Track: 120 city-owned sites the city has named for…
item.content:encoded:
In May, Mayor Mamdani and Deputy Mayor Bozorg put out Block by Block, the administration’s housing plan. The part that matters most for us is the LIFT list, short for Land Inventory Fast Track: 120 city-owned sites the city has named for housing, 50,970 homes in all. None has been built yet. Two are in CB6, Gowanus Green and the Brooklyn Marine Terminal, and we supported both.

We’ve mapped the whole list so you can see it the way we do: by community board, by council district, by agency, by how far along each site is, and set against what every district actually built over the last decade, how rents moved, and what got rezoned. CB6’s own ten-year record works out to about one new home for every forty people living here, most of it from the Gowanus rezoning. The plan is blunt about why the city is short: the 1961 rezoning cut housing capacity by 80 percent, and the tools that followed were too often used to keep people out of the neighborhoods with the most to offer.

See the plan block by block →

Building and preserving affordable housing is CB6’s number one district need, and a list of 120 is a list that can be 121. So on August 12 I wrote to Deputy Mayor Bozorg and DCAS Commissioner Kitasei asking that they add one: 250 Baltic Street, the building the CB6 office is in. Directly above my desk, in fact.

The case is simple. It’s a five-story, 33,750-square-foot building the city owns and DCAS runs. The four floors above us have been empty for a couple of years, since the South Beach Psychiatric Center program and Families First day care moved out. It’s zoned R6 with a C1-3 overlay, so housing needs no rezoning. It went up in 1936, the floor area already exists, and the Bergen Street F/G is a block east on Smith Street. What’s left is conversion work, kitchens, bathrooms, accessibility, which isn’t trivial, but when vacant lots cost multiple millions, an existing structure is a net positive. It sits in the Cobble Hill Historic District, so the exterior would go through Landmarks; personally I think the Department of Health lettering at the top looks sharp.

The building’s recent history makes the argument for it. Twice since the other tenants left, Con Edison has come close to shutting off the power, not over a dispute, but because they didn’t think anyone was here. A city that has functionally forgotten a building is a city that can afford to put people in it. There is no tenant to displace and no service to disrupt. The Carroll Gardens Library returns to its real home later this year, and I’m happy to move the CB6 office; the money is in the budget, and we can’t fit a big meeting in this room anyway.

There’s older history too. In December 1998, the City Council overrode Mayor Giuliani’s veto of a shelter bill sponsored by Councilman Stephen DiBrienza, whose 39th District included 250 Baltic. The Mayor’s office responded by sending eviction notices to every occupant of the building so it could be used as a shelter, with nothing done to make it habitable for anyone. The Times called it a political vendetta. The eviction was rescinded and the proposal dropped. None of those objections apply now, and there’s something poetic about a building once used as a pawn in a policy of pettiness ending up as permanently affordable housing.

A one-bedroom in this district can approach $5,000 a month, to say nothing of what it costs to buy. The city needs more housing, especially affordable housing, wherever and whenever it can build it. Hopefully that includes 250 Baltic Street. We’ve put the full record for the lot online, zoning and what it allows, ownership, permit history, and what’s around it, along with the letter.

250 Baltic Street, the full card → · Read the letter · See it on Instagram

Take a look, and let me know what you think.

item.title: Heating, Voting, Cooling
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: The city has declared a heat emergency as temperatures climb, a new CB6 cooldown page maps surface heat block by block, and last week’s primary winners are confirmed.
item.content:encoded:
Not that it’s been chilly, but it’s hot and expected to get hotter. The city has declared an emergency, and the mayor has issued an executive order to increase protections for people who work outdoors. Official heat safety information is available at nyc.gov/beattheheat or by calling 311.

I built a CB6-focused page earlier this week, which can be viewed at bkcb6.app/cooldown. The page includes cooling centers and resources, a heat vulnerability map, and, thanks to a mapping obsession and other publicly available data, a surface heat map of CB6. I was surprised to learn that about four-fifths of CB6 sits above the citywide average for surface heat. If you have a chance to check it out, let me know what you think.

Moving on to non-temperature-related matters, I’d like to congratulate the winners of last week’s election. In CB6, I congratulate Assembly Member Jo Anne Simon, who won the primary for the 52nd Assembly District. CB6 overlaps with about half of the 52nd, and she won that portion with 69% of the vote compared to her 71% district-wide. I must also congratulate someone who has held other titles, but I’ll focus on the title of “former CB6 member”: Brad Lander, who won the primary for NY’s 10th Congressional District. 100% of CB6 overlaps with NY10, and Brad received 66% of the vote across NY10 but 78.1% of the vote in CB6. I did a deeper dive on this, and elections across the city, at bkcb6.app/2026primary.

I’ll offer one more congrats, and that is to CB6 member Brandon West on his reelection as the president of the Park Slope Food Coop at last night’s annual meeting. On that note, I’ll stop congratulating and start suggesting by another name.

I recommend reading the rest of this email, where you’ll find things like the just-passed city budget and more. No matter what you do, do so in the coolest confines you can find.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201

item.title: Turnout Time
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Primary election day in CB6, with Congress, State Comptroller, and the State Legislature on the ballot and nine of ten eligible voters yet to cast a ballot.
item.content:encoded:
Today, Tuesday, June 23, is primary election day. Congress, State Comptroller, and the State Legislature are on the ballot, and polls are open until 9 PM. I don’t believe there’s been any direct research on this, but if you receive and read community board newsletters, you probably know that. It’s also comparably probable that you haven’t voted.

I say that not as a judgment but as a reality: with 7,749 votes cast in CB6 during early voting, 9 out of 10 eligible CB6 primary voters have not yet voted. This represents 47% of last year’s CB6 early vote total. A drop-off like that isn’t unusual, but unlike the earth’s orbit, we can actually change it.

In fact, the most comparable recent election is the 2022 primary, when all of CB6 was within a competitive congressional district during the first year of a new mayoral administration. Turnout in that year’s primary was 26.2%, or 18,659 votes, across CB6. I’m confident that number will be higher once the polls close tonight, so if you want to be part of outvoting a prior year’s turnout and help make my prediction correct, but need a quick who, what, and where before heading to the polls, go to bkcb6.app/poll-finder-bk.

Some may read all of that and shrug. I don’t blame you; democracy for democracy’s sake can sound broadly appealing, but not necessarily motivating. In the simplest terms, not voting gives someone you disagree with a larger share of influence than they earned. That’s admittedly a bit negative or “hater” framework for civic participation, but it doesn’t make it wrong.

Think of a person, real or imagined, whose views are the opposite of your own. By not voting, you’re effectively giving them a little more say by making their one vote a greater percentage of the votes cast. I’ll use myself as an example. I vote in this district and already have. Those who read my writing or have spoken with me have a sense of my views and CB6’s positions. I know some people strongly disagree with those positions, and that’s perfectly fine. I’d encourage you to use that as motivation, if only to prevent my vote from representing a bigger piece of the electoral pie than it should. You’ve got until 9 PM to do so.

In addition to voting, I’d suggest one other thing: read the rest of this email. No matter what you do, or don’t do, I wish you well.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201

item.title: Today, Tuesday, Totals
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: A Father’s Day note on the final hours of early voting, the closed primary, and why the June primary effectively decides most CB6 elections.
item.content:encoded:
I hope you’ve enjoyed the first hours of summer, and to all the dads out there, happy Father’s Day. While I can’t offer gifts, ties, golf clubs, or any of the other usual dad-themed accessories, perhaps take solace in the fact that we’ve got more than a week before sunsets are earlier than 8:30 PM and that you’ve still got until 5 PM today to vote early.

While I’d strongly encourage you to vote early if you haven’t already, especially since there is no voting tomorrow, Tuesday, June 23, is Primary Election Day, with polls open from 6 AM to 9 PM. If all you need to know is where to vote and what’s on your ballot, particularly since early voting locations differ from Election Day polling sites, head to bkcb6.app/poll-finder-bk.

Turnout is trailing last year’s mayoral primary. That’s not exactly surprising, but it’s also not a particularly good excuse. That goes for everywhere, but especially within CB6, where every primary voter has a competitive congressional race on their ballot. Everyone will also vote in the state comptroller primary, and roughly half of CB6 has a state assembly primary as well. A reminder: this is a closed primary, open only to registered Democrats. It’s also the only party with a primary overlapping CB6.

If you’re reading this and thinking you’ll just wait until November, it’s worth remembering that historically, and likely for the foreseeable future, the primary is where most elections in CB6 and much of Brooklyn are effectively decided. In CB6, for example, Democrats have a registration advantage of 79% to Republicans’ 4%. That’s not a statement of ideology or preference. It’s simply an observation about electoral reality. To put it another way, no Republican, Conservative, or similar candidate has cracked 20% of the vote in CB6’s orbit in years. And the last Republican presidential candidate to carry Brooklyn, and even then by plurality and not majority, was Calvin Coolidge in 1924.

Hopefully some combination of summer solstice daylight, Father’s Day, and what I believe qualifies as dad-coded Brooklyn history has you ready to vote and ready to keep reading the rest of this email, which includes a heavenly seventh, gardens, markets, meetings, and more.

item.title: Civic Inspiration, Guilt & More
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: The Knicks championship parade fills the Canyon of Heroes, early voting lags last year’s pace, and a standing gripe about Madison Square Garden’s tax exemption.
item.content:encoded:
Unless you’re the GOAT of ignoring and avoiding the sights and sounds around you while somehow still reading Community Board emails, you’re aware the New York Knicks are NBA Champions. It’s also likely you’re aware that a ticker-tape parade is taking place today, Thursday, June 18. It gets underway around 10 a.m., and my understanding is that if you want a chance to see the champs, you should’ve already arrived somewhere along the Canyon of Heroes. (Update: I had to reschedule and edit this email as the viewing areas are already full and nobody else will be allowed in.) For more information, like the route map I enjoyed making, where to watch online, and lower Manhattan being car-free (like the Carroll Street Bridge!), go to bkcb6.app/knicks.

If, like me, even before they stopped letting people into the parade, it seemed like a case of “nobody goes there anymore, it’s too crowded,” while still wanting to be part of what theologian Michael Novak called our “civil religion,” I’d suggest voting this morning and getting a Knicks-themed “I Voted” sticker.

Citywide, early voting is running at about 40% of last year’s primary pace. In CB6, we’re running at roughly 49% of where we were at this same point in last year’s primary. So while CB6 is, in turnout terms, outperforming the city as a whole, we’re still only at about half of last year’s turnout. Including today, there are five days left to vote: four days of early voting and Primary Election Day on Tuesday, June 23. If that dual attempt to inspire and guilt one into participating in democracy worked, but you’re wondering where to do so, head to bkcb6.app/poll-finder-bk.

I’ll stop here and suggest you scroll down and read the rest of this email. You’ll find there are lots of things to do as we face Knickless nights ahead.

P.S. A championship, especially since there have only been two between the Knicks and Rangers since the exemption was granted in 1982, doesn’t offset the fact that Madison Square Garden shouldn’t be exempt from property taxes. I’ve ranted about this for years, and so I figured I’d mention it today.

item.title: Today, Tonight & Lines Anew
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope all is well on this 22nd day of January. I've got reminders, a recap, a wonky update with a practical deadline, and some suggestions.
item.content:encoded:
I hope all is well on this 22nd day of January. I've got reminders, a recap, a wonky update with a practical deadline, and some suggestions.

First, reminders: tonight at 630 PM, our Landmarks committee will meet to review one landmark application. Outside our immediate orbit, starting at 6 PM, there's an Atlantic Yards meeting.

Second, the recap: our Transportation Committee met at Middle School 51 (MS51), with Doug Gordon chairing during a short break from his bestselling book tour. Most of the meeting was dedicated to the 5th Ave Business Improvement District (BID) presenting its vision plan, followed by discussion and questions. There were some skeptical questions, but overall, the plan was well received. 

I'd guess some read that and wondered what the vision sees, or what the plan proposes, for 5th Avenue, so I'll summarize as best I can. The Vision Plan outlines changes to the commercial corridor. It treats Fifth Avenue as a "complete street," with wider sidewalks, shorter crossings, space for outdoor dining, and dedicated zones for buses and deliveries to reduce double parking, while noting the eventual possibility of a dedicated bike and/or bus lane. The plan also incorporates green infrastructure, including rain gardens, to address recurring flooding and provides the Department of Transportation (DOT) with a roadmap for implementation over the coming years that makes it safer, helps small businesses thrive, and is resilient to climate-related changes. This is an ongoing process, and the BID expects to receive feedback and guidance from DOT later in the first half of 2026. I'll be sure to keep you posted on DOT's pending reply, but in the meantime, you can bide your time by reading the full plan and presentation here.

Also, a big thank you to MS 51, my alma mater, for hosting, and to the 5th Avenue BID, especially Executive Director Joanna Tallantire, the team at WXY for presenting, and everyone who contributed to the work behind this vision. The committee also discussed Bergen Street and ideas for upcoming meetings, including updates on the proposed Flatbush Avenue bus lane.

Third, the wonky update and practical deadline hinted at in the first paragraph. Yesterday, a State Supreme Court Judge ruled that New York's 11th Congressional District, which includes all of Staten Island and parts of southern Brooklyn, is unconstitutional for diluting the voting power of Black and Latino voters, and ordered new electoral maps to be drawn by February 6.

While CB6 does not currently overlap with NY11, the new lines could affect who represents you in Congress. At present, all of CB6 is in New York's 10th District and represented by Dan Goldman, but that could change once new maps are adopted, potentially splitting CB6 across multiple districts or into 1 new district; only time will tell. We've had multiple congresspeople representing CB6 previously. Just a few years ago, CB6 had some parts represented by Nydia Velázquez and Yvette Clarke. The share of CB6 in the 2 districts even shifted at points, but kept the same two reps.

I mention all of this not to discuss maps or Congress (despite being a preferred topic), but so that you're aware, especially if you want to vote in June's primary election, because if you're not already enrolled in a political party, or want to switch parties, you have to do so by February 14. That means that if you're among the 14% of unaffiliated voters in CB6 come June, you won't be able to vote and would have to wait until November unless you take action. Anyway, check your registration and to make changes, or register to vote in the first place, go here.

I'll stop here and suggest you scroll and read the rest of this email. Whether you scroll or stop here, I wish you the best and stay warm.

item.title: Alternate Side, Tonight, Tomorrow & Thursday
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: At Brooklyn Community Board 6 (CB6), our first of ten 2026 full board meetings was on Wednesday, January 14th, in-person thanks to our ever-gracious hosts at the Van Alen Institute and virtually via Zoom, courtesy of the marvel that is the…
item.content:encoded:
At Brooklyn Community Board 6 (CB6), our first of ten 2026 full board meetings was on Wednesday, January 14th, in-person thanks to our ever-gracious hosts at the Van Alen Institute and virtually via Zoom, courtesy of the marvel that is the internet.

We were joined by representatives from various levels of government, including city and state legislators (Assembly Member Carroll, Council Members Avilés & Hanif) and city agency representatives. Brad Lander, a former CB6 member, Councilmember, and Comptroller, also joined us. Brad offered a brief overview of the city's finances and thanked us, CB6, for supporting the Court Street bike lane.

Our support for the bike lane, to make a dangerous street much safer, was reinforced earlier in the week, when the court challenge to the project was dismissed. You can read the decision here. The judge dismissed the opponents' concerns as anecdotal, lacking data or context. I've said it in this space before: correlation doesn't mean causation. I'm glad the judge saw that. For more context, check out some "rational" coverage and crashcount.nyc.

Back to our full board meeting, the voting agenda for the evening included four liquor license applications and one land use item. The Business Affairs and Permits portion of the agenda included four liquor license applications, all of which were approved: 520 Henry Street for Bar Bruno, a longstanding Mexican restaurant in Carroll Gardens where a change in ownership required a new license; 424 Van Brunt Street for Pony's NYC, a new cocktail bar with small plates in Red Hook in the former Practice Yoga space; 291 Nevins Street for Hidden Rivers BK, a Gowanus bar featuring a rotating weekly brewery spotlight in the former Tuned/Honey Wheel Bike Shop location; and 56 5th Avenue for Drums & Flats, a wing bar from the owners of Uncle Barry's in Park Slope, replacing the former Alchemy space.

The Land Use item was a Uniform Land Use Review Procedure (ULURP) application for 46 Nelson Street in Red Hook, proposing a rezoning to allow a mixed-use building with Mandatory Inclusionary Housing(MIH). The application was overwhelmingly approved, subject to the project being built as presented, except for incorporating setbacks or shifts in bulk to reduce massing at the street wall, and to fewer studios in favor of more two- and three-bedroom units. Because the site is in Red Hook, it falls within the district of Council Member Alexa Avilés, who joined us earlier in the meeting and noted her support for the application. The proposal now advances to the next stage of ULURP, which means it goes to Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso for review.

Our next Full Board meeting will take place at 6:30 PM on Wednesday, February 11, and, just like the January meeting, it will be in person at the Van Alen Institute, with a virtual option via Zoom.

But before that, in the near term, specifically next week, Monday, January 19, is Martin Luther King Jr. Day. In observance of the holiday, alternate-side parking and mail delivery will be suspended, and schools and government offices will be closed. There will also be events honoring Dr. King's life and legacy. Also, next week, in CB6's immediate orbit, we've got three meetings, all starting at 6:30 PM. First, on Tuesday, January 20, the Youth, Human Services, and Environmental Protection Committee will meet at Principles Café for the Youth Mental Health Workshop. On Wednesday, January 21, the Transportation Committee will meet at MS 51 to discuss the Fifth Avenue Vision Plan. Then, on Thursday evening, January 22, the Landmarks Committee will meet virtually via Zoom.

I'll leave you here and recommend you read the rest of this email, which includes tax preparation resources, some thoughts on a new office, additional meetings, and more.

Whether you read the rest or stop scrolling, I wish you the best.

item.title: Happy Thanksgiving!
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: First, on a practical note, Alternate Side Parking and meters are suspended today, Thanksgiving Day, but not tomorrow, Friday, November 28. I mention it because people often assume ASP is suspended the day after Thanksgiving.
item.content:encoded:
First, on a practical note, Alternate Side Parking and meters are suspended today, Thanksgiving Day, but not tomorrow, Friday, November 28. I mention it because people often assume ASP is suspended the day after Thanksgiving. It usually turns into a banner day for parking summonses. Since we are on the topic of Alternate Side Parking, the 2026 calendar is now available.

Second, the Brooklyn Marine Terminal Scoping environmental review comment period has been extended to March 31. The next scoping meeting is on Monday, in person at Sacred Heart & St Stephen's church from 6:00 PM until 930 PM. I must also thank Senator Gounardes and his team for pushing for and making this extension a reality.

Third, as unanimously approved at last week's CB6 Full Board Meeting, our District Needs Statement is now available to read. I cannot mention it without reiterating what a great job the entire budget committee did, especially Rebecca Kobert and Dillon Shen-Cruz. If you have some time, it is well worth the read. 

Fourth, in my most recent newsletter, some people expressed interest in my breakdown of the election in our district and asked that I share my work as I progress on the larger project. Maybe they were just being polite, but either way, here's a draft of the CB6 portion. 

On that note, I will stop here and wish the best this Thanksgiving. I'll be thankful if you read the rest of this email, but no matter what you do, I wish you and yours the very best.

item.title: Meetings,Votes, CB Breakdown
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Next Tuesday, November 18th, EDC and the Mayor's Office of Environmental Coordination will join a CB6 Committee meeting at the Red Hook Community Justice Center. The focus will be on the Brooklyn Marine Terminal Environmental Impact…
item.content:encoded:
Next Tuesday, November 18th, EDC and the Mayor's Office of Environmental Coordination will join a CB6 Committee meeting at the Red Hook Community Justice Center. The focus will be on the Brooklyn Marine Terminal Environmental Impact Statement. I mention more towards the end, so this could serve as a hook to read what's in between and before i go further, thank you to any veterans reading this.

I'd like to reiterate my congratulations to our incoming Mayor, Zohran Mamdani on being elected our 111th Mayor, as well as to Borough President Reynoso, Council Member Avile, and Council Members Shahana Hanif on their reelections, and to former CB6 member and Land Use Chair Alec Schierenbeck on his work as the executive director of the Charter Revision Commission and the passage of ballot questions 2 through 5.

Some may know I taught political science for years at Brooklyn College. With all the election talk and analysis, I noticed a vacuum that, even if nature abhors it, wasn’t likely to be filled, and that was a breakdown by-community board district. I examined the only items on our ballot that could be deemed competitive or contested, and those were the mayoral race and the three ballot measures, numbered 2 through 4. If you don't recall, in a simplified sense, if approved, Question 2 would create a process to fast-track affordable housing applications, Question 3 would simplify the review process for modest housing proposals, and Question 4 would establish an Affordable Housing Appeals Board.

I’m working on a citywide breakdown, but for now, we’ll stick with the district we know and love, Brooklyn Community Board 6. So, I’ll share what I've got, Zohran Mamdani, as I think most would expect. CB6 overwhelmingly voted for Zohran Mamdani, with 75% of the vote, compared to Andrew Cuomo’s 22% and Curtis Sliwa’s 2%. I wasn’t sure what to expect from the ballot measures, as many people spoke out against them. However, in the end, questions 2 through 4 were approved in CB6, with an average approval rate of 65% to 35%. Specifically, question 2 received 66% approval, while questions 3 and 4 received 65% and 62% approval, respectively. As I love to see, we outpaced the borough and city, which also approved them, and it's a good reminder to have some perspective and that the straw poll one takes just by living may not be reflective of any sort if majority.

The other ballot measures all passed CB6, even the one that failed in the city, one which would’ve had mayoral elections in presidential election years. Personally, I voted for question 6 (and the rest). Still, it’s hard to argue against more turnout when the Mayor-elect and these ballot measures, as individual items, received more votes than any other mayor this century. I’m very encouraged that, like the district, he voted to support these measures that help build housing, which will hopefully be a big part of easing the affordability and housing crisis. Even Jacobin, hardly a supporter of Milton Friedman, endorsed these ballot measures, saying that You Can't Have Social Housing Without Building Housing.

On that note, I’ll shift to my usual fare and remind you that our District Needs Survey remains open and will remain open with no plans to close it. If you haven't yet filed it out, please take a few minutes to do so.

Also, don't forget that our full board meeting is on Wednesday and as mentioned in the opening line. Next Tuesday, we'll have a committee meeting at the Red Hook Justice Center, featuring the NYC Bird Alliance and the BMT EIS, and the day after that, on the 19th, we’ll have a Parks and Transportation Committee Meeting.

I suggest scrolling to read some more, but no matter what, I wish you well.

Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: There Is No Tomorrow
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Despite what this email’s subject says, there is a tomorrow, just not for voting. That’s because today, Tuesday, November 4th, is Election Day, and it's the last day to vote.
item.content:encoded:
Despite what this email’s subject says, there is a tomorrow, just not for voting. That’s because today, Tuesday, November 4th, is Election Day, and it's the last day to vote. Polls are open until 9 PM.

A few Election Day, but not electoral notes: schools (for students) and government offices are closed. There is no trash, recycling, or compost collection, and Alternate Side Parking is suspended.

This year's election includes, as I'm sure you've heard, the Mayor, Comptroller, Public Advocate, Borough President, City Council, and District Attorney. You’ll also be voting on proposed Charter Changes to the city’s land use process, as well as when elections are held. If you’re unsure where you vote, find your polling site and hours at findmypollsite.vote.nyc, and if you want some additional information, a compilation of voter guides is available at bit.ly/voterguides25.

Voting, although only part of democracy, remains a significant factor in determining who gets what and how policy choices affect our day-to-day lives. Your vote and choices aren’t just bubbles on a ballot; they shape the budget, laws and their enforcement, buildings being built, parks, transportation, and all areas of policy and planning, and ultimately determine what the city will be going forward. For example, if different choices had been made in the 1950s, the team that has won the last two World Series, whose path started not just in Brooklyn but at Washington Park and got its name from Brooklynites dodging trolleys in the 19th century, would still play in Brooklyn. But I digress and shift back to the 21st century.

Over nine days of early voting, records were shattered. More than 735,000 New Yorkers have checked in to vote early, which is over four times the total from the 2021 mayoral election, when only 169,879 voters cast their ballots over 9 days of early voting. Brooklyn, the best borough, had the most votes cast. Some say that’s because it is the most populous, but I’m going to ignore that and hope Brooklyn continues to lead.

If, after you’ve voted, you want to make more civic choices, take our District Needs Survey. It takes about five minutes and is available at bit.ly/cb6survey27. Lastly, I suggest scrolling down and reading the rest of this email. Regardless of your reading or voting decisions, I wish you the best.

item.title: Vote, Scope & Meet
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: It’s been a while. Based on how many people have mentioned it, some of you still remember when I wrote one of these every day, 800 days in a row, in fact.
item.content:encoded:
It’s been a while. Based on how many people have mentioned it, some of you still remember when I wrote one of these every day, 800 days in a row, in fact. That was sort of fun, and exhausting, and not something I plan to repeat. It was a streak, and barring a sudden surge in CB funding and staffing, I’m seeking to repeat. As I get back into a writing rhythm, you’ll hear from me a bit more. 

Some know that this pause was mental health-related. If you attended our September full board meeting, you may recall that I spoke about the slow pace of the newsletter, which was tied to that, and that I was starting to feel better. That progress finally came after a diagnosis and new treatments. I’ll reemphasize a point I made then: if you need help, get help. Unfortunately, thanks to our healthcare system, getting such help is often easier said than done.

I’m grateful to everyone who noticed this relative silence and checked in. It’s humbling and heartening to be reminded that people seem to care even when you’re not delivering content to their inbox as regularly. And to those who've upped their unpleasantness, I applaud your consistency.

Now, on to the civic concerns you signed up for. I’ve got five things to highlight before I suggest some scrolling.

First, voting in the general election has started, and while it always matters, this year matters more than most. Early voting is underway and runs through Sunday, November 2. Polls are open most days from 9 AM until 5 PM, with extended hours midweek. Election Day is next Tuesday, November 4, and polls will be open from 6 AM until 9 PM. This election includes citywide offices: Mayor, Comptroller, Public Advocate, Borough President, City Council, District Attorney, and Charter Changes. You can find your polling site and hours at findmypollsite.vote.nyc.

There are also several nonpartisan voter guides available at bit.ly/voterguides25. If anyone has other helpful resources, feel free to send them my way. I’m collecting materials for those looking to learn more before heading to the polls.

Second, our FY27 District Needs Assessment Survey is open. Each fall, community boards submit a District Needs Statement to help shape next year’s city budget. Your input helps us set priorities for housing, climate resilience, transportation, parks, and more.

You can take the survey at bit.ly/cb6survfy27.

The survey also includes links to last year’s FY26 District Needs Statement and Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso’s 2025 Comprehensive Plan for Brooklyn. I find the two complement each other well when looking for macro and micro trends. Maybe one day, as we’ve long supported, we’ll have a comprehensive citywide planning model to work from, but I digress.

Third, congratulations to CB6 Transportation Chair Doug Gordon on the publication of his new book, Life After Cars. I’ve put in a request to have it stocked at the 250 Baltic Street Pop-up Library, but it’s popular and there’s already a waiting list.

Fourth, our Business Affairs and Licenses Committee meets tonight at 6:30 PM, Monday, October 27, at 250 Baltic Street to review three liquor license applications. The first is for 238 Court Street, between Kane and Baltic, where an Italian restaurant will take over Sam’s. The second is for 482 Court Street, between Nelson and Luquer, and will feature small plates and wine. The third is for 550 Court Street, between West 9th and Garnet, and will be an Indian restaurant.

﻿

Fifth, two of the three scheduled scoping hearings for the Brooklyn Marine Terminal will be held this week. The first is Tuesday, October 28, from 6:00 to 9:30 PM at the Joseph Miccio Cornerstone Community Center Gym, located at 110 West 9th Street. The second is Thursday, October 30, from 4:00 to 6:00 PM, and will be held virtually. For anyone who cannot make it this week or loves attending meetings, the third hearing is scheduled for Monday, December 1, from 6:00 to 9:30 PM at Sacred Hearts and St. Stephen Church, 125 Summit Street. Public comments are due by December 11. 

Registration links and additional information are available at edc.nyc/bmt. These hearings are also listed on our calendar, along with one of our most frequently visited links, the Brooklyn Marine Terminal materials folder.

I appreciate you reading this far and suggest scrolling to read the rest, but even if you don’t, I wish you the best.

Related tools

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Votes, Meetings, Readings
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope you’re well — and have been well — as I start the newsletter back up. As newsletters of yore, I’ll walk through some recent and upcoming civic matters, share a few reminders and suggestions, and call it a day.
item.content:encoded:
I hope you’re well — and have been well — as I start the newsletter back up. As newsletters of yore, I’ll walk through some recent and upcoming civic matters, share a few reminders and suggestions, and call it a day.

Looking back to last Wednesday, we held our June Board meeting at P.S. 133, where all agenda items were approved, including two landmark applications and an enhanced two-way protected bike lane for Union Street.

Now, this week, we’ve got two CB6 meetings. Tonight - Monday, June 16th at 6:30 PM - our Business Affairs Committee will meet at 250 Baltic Street to review liquor license applications. Then on Wednesday, June 18th at 6:30 PM, our Transportation Committee will meet in person at 250 Baltic Street and over Zoom to hear from the Department of Transportation about proposed pedestrian and bicycle safety improvements for Court Street and a planned bus lane for Flatbush Avenue.

Also of note, the Brooklyn Marine Terminal Task Force vote has been rescheduled for June 27 - a shift from the previously announced June 18 date. It’s been great to see so many of you accessing the BMT folder on the front page of our website. Please check out our newly added joint statement on housing, signed by Senator Gounardes, Council Member Hanif, Assembly Member Simon, the Red Hook East & West Resident Associations, the Fifth Avenue Committee, the Carroll Gardens Association, and the Cobble Hill Association.

And speaking of votes: early voting is underway for the 2025 primary elections, which include races for Mayor, Comptroller, Public Advocate, and City Council. You can vote early through Sunday, June 22, or on Tuesday, June 24, Election Day. Polls are open today from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m.Not sure where to vote? Visit findmypollsite.vote.nyc to confirm your polling location.

On that note, I’ll let you start your day - and I suggest reading the rest of this email. But whether you read it all, just this part, or none at all, I wish you the best.

item.title: Salt, Meet, Listen
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope all is well on this snowy February CB6 Full Board Meeting Eve. I've' got a few items to review.
item.content:encoded:
I hope all is well on this snowy February CB6 Full Board Meeting Eve. I've' got a few items to review. 

First, 1 to 4 inches of snow will accumulate by Wednesday morning. DSNY has issued a Winter Operations Advisory; functionally, it's advised to stay off the roads. DSNY salt spreaders will brine the city streets and, later, plow them if more than 2 inches of snow has accumulated. Additionally, Alternate Side Parking is suspended tomorrow, Wednesday, February 12th. 

Second, keeping with the theme that is tomorrow, our Full Board meeting is tomorrow, Wednesday, February 12th, at 6:30 PM. It will be held in a hybrid format: virtually via Zoom and in person at the Van Alen Institute. The agenda has two applications for Landmark Certificates of Appropriateness and four for on-premises liquor licenses. If you have something better to do than attend our meeting but still crave community board content, listen to WNYC's Morning Edition this Thursday, February 13th, as I'm scheduled to be on air discussing community boards, specifically Friday's deadline.

Third, as was the case the last time I typed in this space, considering the weather, now is as good a time as any to take the Cobble Hill AssocAssociation'sTWaterfront Redevelopment survey, read over all the materials the task force has received and other items at bit.ly/bmtcb6cha. If you've already done that, please check back soon, as we'll be adding more materials.

On that note, I'll let you stay warm while you read the rest of this email. I wish you the best, no matter what you read.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Snow, Survey, Sports
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: February’s first weekend is slated to see snow and the commercial celebration, which is the Super Bowl. I had been rooting for Eli Manning to be named a Hall of Famer last night, but that didn’t happen, so I’ll resume rooting against all…
item.content:encoded:
February’s first weekend is slated to see snow and the commercial celebration, which is the Super Bowl. I had been rooting for Eli Manning to be named a Hall of Famer last night, but that didn’t happen, so I’ll resume rooting against all things Philadelphia. Since I doubt anyone reads this for my thoughts on sports, I’ll be brief and shift to civics. 

First, DSNY has issued a Snow Alert for tomorrow, Saturday, February 8th, beginning at 1:00 p.m. A wintry mix is expected to start things off, followed by snow in the evening. The heaviest snowfall is expected between 7 p.m. and midnight, with an accumulation of between 3 and 5 inches. 

Second, considering the weather, it’s as good of a time as any to take the Cobble Hill Association’s BMT Waterfront Redevelopment survey and read over all the materials the task force has received and other items we’ve been adding at bit.ly/bmtcb6cha. 

Third, thanks to everyone who has contacted me with ideas regarding charter revisions, including encouragement to repeal the “Mistake of 98.” I’ll discuss this further during our Full Board meeting at the Van Alen Institute on Wednesday, February 12th, at 6:30 p.m. 

I’ll stop here and recommend that you read the rest. I wish you the best no matter what you do or who you root for. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: BMT, CRC, ETC
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope February's first four days have been favorable for you. If not, the following items could help turn things around.
item.content:encoded:
I hope February's first four days have been favorable for you. If not, the following items could help turn things around.

First, have you taken the Cobble Hill Association(CHA) survey on the Brooklyn Marine Terminal (BMT) Waterfront Redevelopment yet? Please do so as soon as possible if you haven't already done so. We(CB6 and CHA) are partnering as BMT Task Force members to circulate and analyze the results, so we encourage all neighborhoods to participate. To see all the documents and information we've received as task force members, go to bit.ly/bmtcb6cha. 

Second, our next full board meeting will be held on Wednesday, February 12th, starting at 6:30 PM. It will be held in a hybrid format: in person at Van Alen and virtually on Zoom. It will include votes on liquor licenses and landmark applications. For more information, go to bit.ly/CB6Feb12FB.

Third, falling into the category of last but not least, two weeks ago, Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso appointed me to the New York Council's Charter Revision Commission(CRC). I'm incredibly thankful to BP Reynoso for this opportunity. A common reaction to the announcement has been, "Congrats. What's a CRC, and what does it do?" so I'll do my best to answer those questions. The charter is the city's governing document (consider it the city's constitution). When a CRC is formed, it reviews the charter and then makes recommendations that are voted on in the general election, as has happened in 1898, 1901, 1938, 1963, 1975, 2018, and 2024.

In 2024, you may remember that there were six questions in addition to your ballot having the presidential, federal, and state legislature elections. Questions 2 through 6, which increased the mayor's power regarding public safety, budget, and oversight, resulted from a CRC; 4 of 5 were approved, and unless you are intensely involved with implementing changes, you probably haven't heard or thought much about them since. 

That isn't to say those charter revisions won't have an impact, but some have resulted in things we deal with daily. For example, In 1898, New York City became New York City by consolidating into five boroughs after being approved by voters. With almost 130 thousand people voting, Brooklyn approved the measure with a margin of only 267 votes. Some, occasionally including myself, referred to this as the "mistake of 98" well into the 20th & 21st centuries. Another example would be the creation of community boards(CB) and the Uniform Land Use Review Process (ULURP), as we know them, which resulted from a CRC in 1975. 

You may wonder what this CRC will recommend and when those recommendations will be on the ballot. Other than not reversing the" mistake of 98," I don't know, and on timing, due to a concurrent Mayoral CRC, they'll be on the ballot either this year or next. However, regardless of timing, I can tell you three things I'll be focused on: comprehensive planning, CB reform, and hearing from you. So, let me know if you have any ideas, suggestions, comments, or questions. While we're letting each other know things. I'll share that I've been preparing by reading, re-reading, and compiling related materials and placing them in a folder at bit.ly/crcreading. 

That's enough typing for today, so I'll stop here. I suggest you scroll down and read the rest of this email, but I wish you the best no matter what you decide. 

Related tools

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Firsts
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Hopefully, this first full week of 2025 has been a good one. It was certainly a cold and active one with congestion pricing finally starting, the Mayor’s State of the City address, and our Full Board Meeting.
item.content:encoded:
Hopefully, this first full week of 2025 has been a good one. It was certainly a cold and active one with congestion pricing finally starting, the Mayor’s State of the City address, and our Full Board Meeting.

Our Full Board meeting on Wednesday at Van Alen & via Zoom had three items up for a vote: 2 landmark applications and 1 Liquor License, which were all approved. The first landmark application was for 14 Sterling Place, allowing for a rear yard extension, mechanical equipment on the roof, and facade renovations. The second was for a new four-unit building at 28 7th Avenue. The liquor license application was for a French/ American restaurant at 305 Smith Street. Along with those votes, we were joined by reps from our city, state, and federal governments; there were reminders for upcoming meetings, BMT workshops, concrete on Columbia Street, Community Board applications, Mulchfest, Gowanus construction, our ever-popular Alternate Side Parking Calendar and more.

You’ll find more items of interest by scrolling and reading the rest of this email. But before you do that, I want to highlight that today is the second anniversary of Sarah Schick’s death and that at 5 PM today, there will be a vigil, organized with her family, at the corner of 9th Street and 2nd Avenue to honor her. Some may recall that Sarah was a 37-year-old mother of 2 who was killed by a box truck driver while cycling at the intersection of 9th Street and 2nd Avenue in Gowanus. Sarah’s death, and others, would’ve been avoided had better policy choices been made. Policy choices we’ve long supported, specifically on 9th Street and beyond, such as expanded – and unobstructed – sidewalks and pedestrian islands, continuously protected bike lanes, universally daylighted intersections, and dedicated enforcement of dangerous driving and parking behaviors. There have been some, but not nearly enough, improvements on 9th Street in the intervening years, but we shouldn’t have to wait for tragedy for those design and enforcement improvements to happen. Making those changes would save lives and honor Sarah’s memory. 

On that note, whether you read past this point or not, I wish you the best. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Last Chance to Vote! Polls are open until 9 pm
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: As I'm sure you already know, today is Election Day. The polls are open until 9 p.m.
item.content:encoded:
As I'm sure you already know, today is Election Day. The polls are open until 9 p.m. Big compliments to the election workers who woke up early enough to open the polls at 6 a.m. Please note that schools and government offices are closed, there will be no trash recycling or compost collection, and Alternate Side Parking is suspended today.

Election day is your last chance to vote and determine who the next president is and who represents you in both houses of our federal and state legislatures and ballot proposals. The first of those ballot proposals is for the Equal Rights Amendment, which, if approved, would create constitutional protections against discrimination based on ethnicity, national origin, age, disability, and sex—including sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, pregnancy, and pregnancy outcomes, and reproductive healthcare and autonomy.

Those are great reasons to vote, but since you're likely in Brooklyn if you're reading this, voting today means you'd also be doing your part to ensure the best borough is also the best at voting. I mean that New York City's early voting totals, with 1.1 million votes already cast, almost set a new record, and Brooklyn's 345 thousand voters were the most of any borough. So please do your part and vote.

Speaking of you doing your part, there's an official drought watch. That doesn't mean being a spectator; we can all use less water. 

Of course, there's more than elections and droughts happening. There are grants, films, trees, markets, murals, surveys, our Full Board meeting next Wednesday, November 13th, and more. If you read the rest, you'll see what I'm referring to.

﻿No matter what you do, I hope it includes voting, but no matter what, I wish you the best.

Related tools

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Vote, Fall, Run
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Hopefully, your November is off to a good start. To maintain or improve this start, you can vote, jaywalk, sleep more, or cheer on folks running through CB6 and across the city.
item.content:encoded:
Hopefully, your November is off to a good start. To maintain or improve this start, you can vote, jaywalk, sleep more, or cheer on folks running through CB6 and across the city.

What I mean is that polls are open until 5 pm today and tomorrow; you can now legally cross the street wherever you please, and the New York City Marathon course includes our district's segment of 4th Avenue. Streets on the course won't be open for cars from around 7 am until the afternoon, depending on the location. 4th Avenue is expected to reopen around 2:20 pm. CB6's Business Affairs and Licensing chair, Mandi Spishak‑Thomas, will be among those running. Best of luck to Mandi! If anyone needs more motivation to cheer her and others on, remember that many will enjoy the marathon at locations whose liquor license was approved by her committee.

For many, civic concerns can be difficult to consider beyond Tuesday's election, so I'll wrap this up. However, I recommend reading the rest of this email because you'll see a community looking to a future beyond the election, which gives me hope.

No matter what you do, I wish you the best and make sure to vote.

Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: Votes, Parades, Moonshots, Meetings & More
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I intended to send a newsletter last night but got distracted by Stanton's moonshot and the fact that Nestor is not ready. On that note, I'm ready to write about some civic matters, so I'll get to it.
item.content:encoded:
I intended to send a newsletter last night but got distracted by Stanton's moonshot and the fact that Nestor is not ready. On that note, I'm ready to write about some civic matters, so I'll get to it. 

First, early voting has begun. It takes place from now through Sunday, November 3rd. Polling sites open at 8 am and close at 5 pm on Saturdays, Sundays, and 8 pm, Monday through Friday. On Tuesday, November 5th, election day, polls will be open from 6 am until 9 pm. To find out where to vote, go to findmypollsite.vote.nyc. To learn more about who and what you'll vote for, go to nycvotes.org.

item.title: Update- Saturday, June 29,2024
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope you're enjoying the weekend. It follows quite a week for civics, from macro to micro: a debate, an election, a budget, and meetings, two of which were our committees.
item.content:encoded:
I hope you're enjoying the weekend. It follows quite a week for civics, from macro to micro: a debate, an election, a budget, and meetings, two of which were our committees. 

The first of our meetings was on Monday when our Permits & Licenses committee unanimously approved two liquor license applications. One is for a Mexican restaurant on 2nd Street between 4th and 5th (previously Benchmark), and the other is for an Argentinian restaurant at 550 Court Street, off West 9th.  

Then, on Thursday, DOT presented plans for a Flatbush Ave Bus Lane to our Transportation & Public Safety Committee. We made our preference for a center-running bus lane clear to DOT, especially after having the slow bus speeds documented in the presentation. However, we didn't vote on this since it's still in the preliminary stages, but we expect DOT to come back to us with more fleshed-out plans in the fall. During the meeting, we acknowledged the tragic death of Carolyn Cox, an 83-year-old woman who was struck and killed by a dump truck on Wednesday where Bond and Butler Street meet. As we said on Wednesday, this tragedy underscores the pressing need to design all of our streets with safety in mind, including features like physical curb extensions, clearly marked and raised crosswalks, and universal daylighting, and to implement the lower speed limits facilitated by the recent passage of Sammy's Law as soon as possible and that our thoughts are with the victim and her family and friends. 

I'll stop and suggest scrolling to read the rest of this email. But before that, I'll highlight that the City's FY25 budget, as we voted for, will include an additional 2 billion dollars for affordable housing. We'd have preferred more money, but this part of the budget is a step in the right direction. 

Whether you read past this point or not, I wish you the best.

item.title: Update- Sunday, June 9,2024
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: The week went well in CB6 as Rebecca Kobert joined our staff as Land Use Coordinator. We had other excellent applicants for the role.
item.content:encoded:
The week went well in CB6 as Rebecca Kobert joined our staff as Land Use Coordinator. We had other excellent applicants for the role. Still, I feel, and others who have met with her have agreed, that Rebecca’s experience with CB6 and her familiarity with land use policy make her perfect for the role. While we know CB6 is already the happiest district in the city, adding Rebecca to the staff makes me hopeful that the district could end up even happier. 

Outside of CB6, things are looking far less happy and hopeful, thanks to Governor Hochul. If it’s unclear, I’m referring to the 11th-hour “postponement” of congestion pricing(CP), which we and all elected officials overlapping with CB6 have supported for years. The way this was done (video fiat?) is the type of thing that, even among those who oppose CP, can make one lose faith in the government’s ability to do anything. I don’t think anyone is certain of what will happen, but Hellgate and Streetsblog have good overviews of where we stand, including ways to take action and have your voice heard. 

Lastly, a reminder that our June Full Board meeting is this Wednesday, June 12th, at 6:30 PM, and the in-person portion will NOT BE AT THE VAN ALEN INSTITUTE. So, for the first time since the pandemic, the in-person option will be at New York Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital at 506 6th St, while the virtual option is, as always, over Zoom. 

I’ll stop typing and suggest scrolling to read the rest of this email. If you do, you’ll learn about Alternate Side Parking, the Southwest Brooklyn Tenant Union’s Good Cause Eviction event, and more.

Whether you do or don’t read the rest, I wish you the best.

item.title: Sunday, May 19, 2024
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Hopefully, your weekend’s going well thus far. It follows a week that saw a big announcement for Red Hook and a forward-thinking discussion on 4th Avenue.
item.content:encoded:
Hopefully, your weekend’s going well thus far. It follows a week that saw a big announcement for Red Hook and a forward-thinking discussion on 4th Avenue.

The Red Hook announcement was a land swap with the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey that will give the NYC government control of the South Brooklyn Marine Terminal. The stated mixed-use goals(reducing truck traffic, housing, retail, green space, and a modern port) are a step in the right direction, and hopefully, that will remain the case as details and the process are made clearer. 

The discussion I referred to the discussion on 4th Avenue was a meeting held by Forth on Fourth Ave (FOFA) on Wednesday night at the Old Stone House. It was a great discussion on what the community wants on 4th Avenue and what’s happening regarding traffic safety, flooding, and design. SJ Avery and Grace Freedman did a great job organizing the meeting and conducting the community survey, which informed much of the discussion. The discussion included Council Members Hanif and Aviles, DDC, DSNY DEP, CB6 ( represented by myself and our transportation chair, Doug Gordon), GCC, and many others. Improving 4th Avenue is certainly an ongoing conversation, so there will be more opportunities to discuss. However, if you missed out this week, you can see the survey and presentations from the meeting here. 

In keeping with the theme of community meetings, please keep in mind that this Thursday, May 23rd, we have a Landmarks/ Land Use committee meeting that includes the City of Yes Housing Opportunity. It’ll be in person at the Van Alen Institute and virtually via Zoom. 

I’ll stop here and suggest you read the rest of this email. No matter what you do, I wish you the best. Let’s go, Rangers and Knicks.
