item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well as we brace for the, metaphorical, impact that is tomorrow's election. 

Early voting is complete and over a million votes were cast early and in person across the 5 boroughs. I haven’t seen a breakdown within the Boroughs yet but Brooklyn had 373,270 votes which was over 134 thousand more than the second place borough, Manhattan. So all that’s left to close the books is old fashioned “Election Day” which is tomorrow, Tuesday November 3rd. Polls will be open from 6 am until 9 pm. If you’re voting absentee and haven’t yet mailed your ballot don't mail it, but instead drop it off at any polling site.

But that is tomorrow and there’s still some stuff happening tonight and plans for, assuming the sun rises, things happening beyond tomorrow. Some are listed below my email signature and I recommend checking them out.

Either way, stay safe and enjoy the rest of your first November Monday.

item.title: Last Chance To Vote Early!
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope everyone got to enjoy the extra hour of sleep as we squandered daylight. Remember, today, Sunday, November 2nd, is the last day of early voting, and polls are open until 5 pm.
item.content:encoded:
I hope everyone got to enjoy the extra hour of sleep as we squandered daylight. Remember, today, Sunday, November 2nd, is the last day of early voting, and polls are open until 5 pm. 

If you haven’t voted already, I suggest you use civic pride as a motivation. Our great borough of Brooklyn has seen the most votes cast so far, and voting today can increase that lead. High turnout is a proud tradition in our community, and there is no reason for it not to continue. For example, my old boss Assemblymember Joan Millman and her successor current 52nd District Assemblymember, Jo Anne Simon, have both received the highest vote totals of any Assemblymember in the state in recent elections. 

It would be great, no matter what person or party you choose for whatever office, that we win the only meaningful participation trophy with the highest voter rates ever.

Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: End of Early Voting, Resolutions, Recaps
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I start today with another CB6 "spoiler." Last night, as previewed in prior newsletters, our Transportation & Public Safety Committee met. During the Public Safety portion of the committee meeting agenda, the new Commanding Officer at the…
item.content:encoded:
I start today with another CB6 "spoiler." Last night, as previewed in prior newsletters, our Transportation & Public Safety Committee met. During the Public Safety portion of the committee meeting agenda, the new Commanding Officer at the 76th Precinct, Vitaliy Zelikov, introduced himself to the committee and "attended" the rest of the meeting.

The transportation portion consisted of an informational presentation and a vote on a resolution from Resilient Red Hook, asking for Van Brunt Street to be removed as a truck route. The committee approved it unanimously with a motion with the amendment that alternative options allow such trucks to drive through the container port to lessen truck traffic on Van Brunt.

This resolution, the liquor license application approved on Tuesday, and the landmarks application from 2 weeks ago, will now move to a full board vote at our November 18th meeting. If you want to relive the magic, you can watch last nights and all our committee meetings from the week on YouTube.

With tomorrow being Halloween, a day when our President makes an exception and joins the rest of us in unequivocally supporting mask-wearing, it's important to note that the other day's matter as COVID-19 numbers are headed in the wrong direction. So, even if you've never worn a mask on Halloween, make sure tomorrow is the first time you do. When wearing the mask, still keep your distance, and maintain all safety protocols.

No matter what you do, I hope you have a good weekend; maybe check out a podcast, but no matter what, stay safe and turn back your clocks! 

Related tools

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.description: Good afternoon, I hope this email finds you well on this 27th day of October. Tonight’s our Permits & Licenses Committee meeting , Chaired by Rachel Freeman. The agenda will focus on reviewing one app
item.content:encoded:
Good afternoon,

I hope this email finds you well on this 27th day of October. Tonight’s our Permits & Licenses Committee meeting , Chaired by Rachel Freeman. The agenda will focus on reviewing one application for an on-premise liquor license. The applicant is  Terrace Restaurant and Bakery Corp. at 280 5th Avenue between Garfield Place & 1st ST), Bklyn, NY 12215. Also, starting at 6:30 PM tonight is the monthly Gowanus CAG meeting.

The second CB6 meeting of the week is tomorrow, Wednesday, October 28th , with our Youth Human Services and Education Committee welcoming School District 15 Superintendent and a great friend to Community Board 6, Anita Skop. The purpose will to discuss the current school year and answer questions folks may have. On Thursday, October 29th, we will cycle through our Transportation & Public Safety Committee meeting with DOT presentations and be introduced to the new Commanding Officer at the 76th Precinct.

Some more happenings and items of interest are listed below, including mask guidelines for the only day anyone tended to wear a mask before COVID, Halloween. Anyway, I hope you check out the rest of the newsletter, and I hope you stay safe and enjoy the rest of your Tuesday.

item.title: Recordings,Recaps, Reality
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well as we close out a busy week, and re-energize over the weekend before we head into yet another busy week.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well as we close out a busy week, and re-energize over the weekend before we head into yet another busy week.

I’ve heard that NYC was slandered on national TV last night being characterized as a "ghost town". Yeah, the Ghostbuster movies are set here, but it’s hardly a “ghost town” in the sense of it being vacant with tumbleweeds instead of bicyclists, pedestrians, and now diners in the streets.

There was one place, even though it was virtual, that was certainly not empty, and that was last night’s CB6 Landmarks/ Land Use meeting. Close to 600 people registered, and close to 400 attended. For those who couldn’t make it or want to relive or review it, click here. When you click, you’ll find a recording of the meetings and the Gowanus presentation that was the focus of the meeting. You’ll also find links to sign up for the two DCP Gowanus precertification meetings that were announced last night. The first for November 19th will focus on Gowanus Green/ Public Place, while the second, on December 2nd, will focus on Gowanus Infrastructure. 

But before those two meetings, and unrelated to any major rezoning, CB6 has three committee meetings next week. All three will begin at 6:30 PM starting on Tuesday when Permits & Licenses meets followed by Youth, Human Services, and Education (YHSE) meeting on Wednesday. Last, but not least, Transportation & Public Safety will meet on Thursday.

Before all that, we’ve gotta get through the weekend, which has some happenings that you can find out about by scrolling down this email. However, before you do that, I’d recommend reading about “reality” and make a plan for voting early.

On that note, I end by saying, stay safe and have a good weekend. Stay safe, scroll down, enjoy the grey, and have a nice night.

item.title: Zooming, Meeting, Electing
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well on this grey day. I know people are focused on tonight’s meeting, but I have a few items to go over before my usual scrolling suggestion beyond my signature.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well on this grey day. I know people are focused on tonight’s meeting, but I have a few items to go over before my usual scrolling suggestion beyond my signature. I’ll begin by informing everyone that the memorial service for community luminary Buddy Scotto, scheduled for November 7th, has been postponed. When any new announcements are made, I will let you know.

Last night, like tonight, was a busy night across our community, but I’ll focus on two things very much in the CB6 orbit. 

First, our very own Joe Ann Brown was elected to replace the incumbent as the Warren Street Tenant Association President after a hard-fought campaign. In the spirit of intensifying civic engagement, there was a record turnout. I was honored to administer this election, and it gives me a tremendous amount of hope for our community. I am excited to continue to work with everyone at Warren Street. 

Secondly, our CB6 Parks & Environmental Protection Committee met and received a capital project update from the City’s Parks Department, followed by a presentation from Brooklyn Heat/Cool Smart. A big thank you to everyone who presented and to our Environmental Protection Co-Chair Angelica Ramdhari for handling zoom hosting duties. You can see both presentations here, as well as a recording of the meeting.

Just like our Parks & Environmental meeting, tonight’s Landmarks/Land Use meeting will be recorded and shared on our YouTube page and tomorrow’s newsletter. This is one final reminder that tonight’s meeting begins at 6 PM. Those who want to make public comments or ask questions tonight, please fill out this form. We will get to as many questions as possible. Please keep in mind that close to 500 people have already registered for the event. Please remember that tonight is an informational session, and there will not be a vote on anything related to the pending rezoning. There will be other opportunities to weigh in. The rezoning will not officially start until next year, but, as the purpose of this meeting indicates, this will help us understand that timeline and the timeline before the official review, aka ULURP.

item.title: Evrémonde, Early, Absentee
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well on this cloudy Tuesday. Some reminders new and old today, but I’ll be as brief as possible.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well on this cloudy Tuesday. Some reminders new and old today, but I’ll be as brief as possible. 

We are two weeks from the state and federal elections, but early voting starts this Saturday, October 24th, and you can still request an absentee ballot until a week from today, on Tuesday, October 27th. One week from today, the CB6 Permits & Licenses committee will review two liquor license applications beginning at 6:30 PM via Zoom.

However, there are still lots of things happening this week, including two CB6 committee meetings. Tomorrow night Wednesday, October 21st, our Parks Committee meets at 6:30 PM, and our Landmarks/Land Use Committee is meeting on Thursday, October 22nd, at 6:00 PM. If you want to submit comments, it’s constructive to do so via our portal, as some have already done.  

Lastly, before my daily recommendation that you read past my email signature, I’d strongly recommend reading the New York Daily News’s cover story from yesterday. The story is about two school districts, and the inequity, based on family income, heightened with our return to school. One of those two districts is our very own District 15. You may recall that this is almost EXACTLY what we, and many others, including teachers and principals, were saying would happen, and now it’s happening. My only hope is that the city listens to educators going forward instead of politicians, so maybe when the next someone cites the “tale of 2 cities,” it’s confirmed they don’t think of Charles Darnay’s uncle as a hero. 

I’ll end here and hope you enjoy the rest of your Tuesday.

item.title: Counting, Commenting, Collecting
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well after what was, hopefully, an enjoyable weekend. There’s lots of stuff happening this week, including two CB6 meetings later this week, so I'll get right to it.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well after what was, hopefully, an enjoyable weekend. There’s lots of stuff happening this week, including two CB6 meetings later this week, so I'll get right to it.

On Wednesday, October 21st, our Parks Committee meets at 6:30 PM, and our Landmarks/Land Use Committee is meeting on Thursday, October 22nd, at 6:00 PM. The Landmarks/Land Use meeting has received some coverage due to the agenda, including a presentation from the Department of City Planning (DCP). That presentation will outline their timeline in advance of the Gowanus rezoning being certified (the first stage of the ULURP) in January 2021. Thank you to everyone who has submitted questions in advance of Thursday’s meeting, and if anyone else wants to, we now have a portal to do so right here.

Before going any further, I want to congratulate the NYC Census 2020 team, including CB6 member Jason Reischel, despite every roadblock imaginable, for matching the 2010 Census self-response rate of 61%. Roadblocks such as a hostile federal government looking to intimidate immigrants into not getting counted, and legal challenges ended up cutting the count short. On top of that, it took place when we in NYC were the epicenter of the pandemic. Even with limited door to door outreach, the NYC Census team still managed to beat the census bureau’s expectations by almost 4 points and did better than cities such as LA, Chicago, Boston, Miami, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Dallas, and Houston. 

I’d take this example as a reminder of why civic participation is so meaningful and never stops. With that, I’ll recommend reading some civic stuff below, such as the Gowanus ArtWalk, and hope that you enjoy the rest of your Monday.

item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well as we head into what is supposed to be, in contrast with today, quite sunny. I prefer rain, but if you're outside, please keep your face covered and your distance as there, as always, are some interesting happening, and I don't think anyone wants to resume a "PAUSE" or mimic Europe’s latest lockdowns. 

You can find those interesting items below my email signature, but before that, I have a few quick CB6 centered reminders that won't require any masking. 

On Wednesday, October 21st, our Parks Committee meets at 6:30 PM, and our Landmarks/Land Use Committee is meeting on Thursday, October 22nd, at 6:00 PM. The Landmarks/Land Use meeting has received some coverage due to the agenda, which will include a presentation from the Department of City Planning (DCP). That presentation will outline their timeline for in advance of the Gowanus rezoning being certified (the first stage of the ULURP) in January 2021.  

While we don't have a confirmed agenda for our Permits & Licenses meeting that would usually be held on the 4th Monday of the month, it will be held instead on the 4TH Tuesday, if it is to take place October 27th. Of course, I'll keep you posted as I think it's understandable that, given the current conditions, there is some reluctance for opening a restaurant or bar and thus applying for a liquor license. 

With that, I'll say have a good weekend, check out stately suggestions in the Brooklyn Paper, and stay safe.

item.title: Meeting, Magic, MEND
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well after last night’s board meeting. It was good to “see” and hear from everyone.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well after last night’s board meeting. It was good to “see” and hear from everyone. I’m sure we, and that very much includes me, will get the “mute/unmute/host function down sooner than later. We had a good turnout with over 150 attendees, including 37 board members, representatives from every government level, and Chairperson Peter Fleming’s ten-week-old puppy, Monte. The voting agenda consisted of passing two recommendations from our Economic, Waterfront, Community Development, and Housing Committee. One was in support of the MEND program, and the other supported affordable housing and by exploring and expanding the development of accessory dwelling units.

You may see those resolutions here, as well as the letter we’d written to DOT in support of a comprehensive traffic study. But, if you want to relive the magic, you can watch the meeting here on YouTube.  

Also, as mentioned last night, we have a few meetings coming up, including next Wednesday’s Parks Committee meeting and Thursday’s Landmark/Land Use meeting, which will include DCP presenting an overview of the timeline for precertification’ plans regarding the pending Gowanus Neighborhood rezoning. 

Before telling you to keep reading below my signature, I’d like to congratulate 2 CB6 board members. Firstly congrats to John Heyer on being part of Governor Cuomo’s commission for the Mother Cabrini statue that was recently unveiled at the start of Italian Heritage Month. Secondly, congrats to David Briggs’s architecture firm LOCI Architecture which received a 2020 Lucy G. Moses Preservation Award.

Some things are happening inside and outside CB6’s sphere of influence listed below my email signature, and I recommend you check them out. 

No matter what, stay safe and enjoy the rest of your Thursday.

item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well as we head into, what is for some, a three day weekend while hoping to contain COVID-19 clusters and stopping any spikes from spreading. 

Of course, to do that, we’ve got to keep our distance and, as they say, “mask up.” This is especially important as there are happenings across our community this weekend, and beyond that, you can find out about by reading past my signature. 

Before that, I’d like to remind you that next Wednesday is our October General board meeting, held via zoom beginning at 6:30 PM. Also, on the CB6 Calendar, the following week is our Landmark/Land Use meeting on Thursday, October 22nd, via zoom. The agenda is still in formation, but kicking off the meeting will be the Department of City Planning discussing some of its precertification plans and the Gowanus Rezoning timeline. If you want to submit questions in advance of the meeting, I’m happy to accept them and pass them along to DCP(they will also take questions during the meeting).

With that, I’ll say have a good weekend, check out some policy suggestions in the Brooklyn Paper, and take note that Alternate Side Parking is suspended through Monday, and trash pick-up is suspended on Monday.

item.description: Once again, if you plan to go anywhere, it's a good idea to check out what COVID-19 zone it's in so you can adjust your plans if necessary. For example, if you have kids or work at one of these 169 school sites, your plan is altered for at…
item.content:encoded:
Once again, if you plan to go anywhere, it's a good idea to check out what COVID-19 zone it's in so you can adjust your plans if necessary. For example, if you have kids or work at one of these 169 school sites, your plan is altered for at least the next two weeks. However, no matter how you strategize to get about keep your distance and wear a mask there are some great things happening across our community. You can check out a bunch of them below my email signature, but I have a couple of things I'd like to mention before that.

First, we have a resumption of our general board meetings with an October zoom meeting next Wednesday, and two weeks from tonight, on Thursday October 22nd, our Landmarks/Land Use meeting will be held, via zoom, starting at 6:00 PM. The agenda is still in formation, but we expect a few landmark items to be up for review. Most notably the Department of City Planning will present at the beginning of the meeting about the Gowanus Rezoning. Specifically, DCP will be discussing some of its pre-certification plans and timeline. This is good news as we've been asking for pre-certification meetings long before the pandemic hit. However, what is presented, and not just the timeline, will ultimately determine our reaction.

item.title: Closure, Community Council, Flu Shots & More
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well this Wednesday as we work to avert a second wave of COVID infections.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well this Wednesday as we work to avert a second wave of COVID infections. 

To that end, the city is set to begin enforcing a series of state-mandated zoned shutdowns of businesses and schools in various “hot spots” in Brooklyn and Queens. As in the spring, the Governor felt it necessary to overrule the city, initially reject the city’s plan and followed it up by offering similarly confusing, arbitrary, and vague plans. 

Maybe by the time you read this, the zones will have been clarified, but the state's guidance are maps that don’t follow the street grid and that slice blocks into chunks without providing searchable tools. Click here to see Brooklyn’s map. 

The latest I had heard is that city is developing a site where you can plug in your address and find out what zone you’re in, but it’s not up yet. As Chalkbeat New York’s Alex Zimmerman pointed out this afternoon, some principals can't tell parents whether their buildings will be open tomorrow. I know from my personal life, teachers, administrators, school staff, parents, and, most importantly, students have to readjust for remote learning the fly, but had the administration listened to teachers in the first place, they would have been properly grounded.

Anyway, I digress to remind you that we have our October General Board Meeting one-week from tonight, fill out the census and make sure you are registered to vote. As usual, there is more to note and possibly attend, such as tonight’s 76th Precinct Community Council meeting chaired by our very own Jerry Armer, listed below my email signature.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Recommending, Mediating
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Despite what some in infinitely higher office than I say, COVID-19 is not the flu, and I don’t mean that in a good way. You should get a flu shot this year, and still, we need to keep our distance and our faces covered throughout October…
item.content:encoded:
Despite what some in infinitely higher office than I say, COVID-19 is not the flu, and I don’t mean that in a good way. You should get a flu shot this year, and still, we need to keep our distance and our faces covered throughout October on all days in addition to Halloween. 

Thankfully, while not as satisfying as in-person, we have zoom and meetings like last night’s CB6 Economic, Waterfront, Community Development & Housing Committee meeting (EWCDH). As previewed in previous newsletters, we had a presentation from OATH Commissioner Joni Kletter on the MEND Program and Bronx CB6 district manager John Sanchez. The committee unanimously approved recommendations based on both presentations. One to support the MEND program, and the other in support of affordable housing and shouldering our fair share of it in a citywide housing crisis. Both of those recommendations will be voted on at next Wednesday’s General Board Meeting. 

If you’d like to relive the magic or see it for the first time, you can watch the meeting on youtube and see the presentation materials from Commissioner Kletter and District Manager Sanchez here.  You can also find notes and information from last week’s Waterfront presentation here. 

As usual, there is more to note and possibly attend listed below my email signature, so I suggest you keep scrolling. 

Either way, stay safe and enjoy the rest of your Tuesday.

item.title: MEND, BX, MORE
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: We start the first full week of October with a lot of activity and cautionary stats across Brooklyn.
item.content:encoded:
We start the first full week of October with a lot of activity and cautionary stats across Brooklyn. 

On Monday, Governor Cuomo announced that roughly 300 schools, both public and private, within nine New York City ZIP codes would shift to entirely remote learning due to a spike in COVID-19 infections. The governor held back on approving the City’s straight forward plan for closings within entire ZIP CODES, saying that “we can draw better lines then a zip code.” While that may be the case, this is coming from a governor who overruled the city on “Shelter In Place” orders in March. According to Columbia University’s public health school, it led to thousands of more deaths than we would have had if we timely instituted a shelter in place directive. 

But I digress and remind everyone to keep a safe distance and cover your face instead of going to in-person and, worse still, mask optional gatherings, be cool, and attend meetings such as tonight's virtual Brooklyn Community Board 6 EWCDH committee meeting. It will feature OATH Commissioner Joni Kletter discussing the MEND program, followed by Bronx CB6 district manager John Sanchez on citywide development needs and issues.

There are more things to note and possibly attend listed below my email signature, so I suggest you keep scrolling. 

Either way, stay safe and enjoy the rest of your Monday.

Best,

item.content:encoded:
With high schools kicking off in-person learning today, we had our last “first day of school’ and with increasing uncertainty. One school has already been shut down but let’s hope it’s the last. Hopefully, we don't see a second shutdown. So please keep your distance, your hands clean, and your face covered.

If not, schools won’t be the only thing closed,Restaurants that are barely hanging on will also end up closed. I don’t think it's possible to overstate how important this is. If you don’t believe me check out State Comptroller Dinapoli’s report on the thousands restaurants, hundreds of thousands of jobs, threatened by this pandemic.

On that note, I'll suggest that you scroll on down for more information; and enjoy the rest of your Thursday and maybe listen to a song that is fitting for today’s date.

item.title: Trains, Transmission, Enfranchise
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well and enjoying this fine Wednesday. I have a few quick items I want to touch on, and then you'll be free of me until next month.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well and enjoying this fine Wednesday. I have a few quick items I want to touch on, and then you'll be free of me until next month. 

First, there was an encouraging drop in COVD-19 testing rates as the latest testing showed positivity of under 1 % instead of the 3.5 we ate that was reported a day earlier. While the good news is nice to hear, it is not yet a cause for celebration or relaxing. If anything, it's a reminder to everyone that we can keep these numbers low if we maintain distance, cover our faces, and follow all safety protocols. It's hardly fun to wear a mask, but I'd wear a mask forever instead of having to live in a shutdown city as we did in the spring or jeopardize another person. 

Speaking of things that were shut down, but aren't now, today Is the first day of indoor dining in NYC since March. There are a lot of safety protocols put into place, including a 25% percent capacity limit. This is only marginally helpful to restaurants; it may be a bridge if ever, our US Senate and President agree to pass necessary funding to help our restaurants. It will also help if Assemblymember Carroll's business interruption bill is signed into law by the Governor. 

I wouldn't necessarily get my hopes up. This is the same Governor who doesn't want to send out corrected absentee ballots to the nearly one hundred thousand voters who received incorrect ballot envelopes right here in Brooklyn. Instead, the Cuomo administration suggests that the Board mail voters just the corrected return envelopes, asking voters to use the ballots they may have already discarded after the first erroneous mailing. I'm naturally cynical, but I hope that not too many people are disenfranchised. 

On that note, I'll suggest that you scroll on down for more information; let me know if you hear of any postal employees selling ballots or throwing them in the Gowanus, and enjoy the rest of your Wednesday.

Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: Ballots, Schools, Certification & RBG from JAS
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well and enjoying the final 48 hours of September. I have a few quick items I want to touch on.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well and enjoying the final 48 hours of September. I have a few quick items I want to touch on.

First, some of the one hundred thousand or so prospective voters who were given mislabeled ballots in our perpetually failing electoral system.have reached out to ask what to do. NYC Board of Elections Executive Director Michael Ryan has announced that all voters who experienced this issue will be sent a new ballot with a letter from the BOE describing the problem. However, to be safe, you can also reach out to the NYC Board of Elections by calling  1-866-VOTE-NY or sending an email to  Apply4Absentee@boe.nyc. This massive "software" error in the final weeks of a crucial election in a turbulent era is unfathomable and unforgivable but somehow unsurprising when it comes to the Board of Election. This goes hand-in-hand with tabulation delays and misplaced tablets.

Second, I hope everyone who was part of in-person learning had a good day and that we continue to stay safe. The citywide testing rate has been low enough, but yesterday it was above 3%, and if that is the case for seven days, the school buildings automatically close. So please, keep your distance and cover your face if not for yourself for others.

Third, while it hasn’t been picked up by any news sources yet, Deputy Mayor Vicki Been referred to the coming certification of a Gowanus rezoning in early 2021 at a City & State conference this afternoon. On the heels of that news, I want to let everyone know that we’re already in discussions to have pre-certification meetings held in accordance with our long standing demands. Of course, pre-certification meetings are positive and will help our community understand what’s in the pending plan. Ultimately, the content of those plans will be subject to a formal review process. The Deputy Mayor also indicated that there are other actions for review forthcoming.

So rest up for the action-filled New Year and enjoy the rest of your Tuesday, stay safe, and check out the items below.

item.description: I hope this email finds you well. For our Jewish readers, as the book closes and your transgressions have been cast away, I hope your fast was easy, and you take full advantage of the clean slate that comes along with a new year.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well. For our Jewish readers, as the book closes and your transgressions have been cast away, I hope your fast was easy, and you take full advantage of the clean slate that comes along with a new year. 

Despite a lack of or perhaps "no," confidence tomorrow is the first day of the in-person learning aspect of the blended school schedule for students Kindergarten through 8th grade. Hopefully, it all comes together and works out, and we wish everyone involved, students, parents, teachers, administrators, and support staff, all the best! 

We, as a city, have made and maintain significant progress on COVID, but there we're not out of the woods, and we've seen some spikes right here in Brooklyn, so please maintain your distance and keep your face covered. If the rates keep rising, we won't see restaurants offering indoor or outdoor dining. I don't think anyone wants to see the further economic collapse and a return to days resembling the awful spring of 2020. 

Anyway, I'll get into more topics as the week goes on but check out the items below, including our EWCDH meeting one week from tonight via zoom.

item.title: Where there's a chance
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well, and just like the first day of fall, I hope this Wednesday has proceeded swimmingly. Perhaps I should say, as swimmingly as 2020 can be.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well, and just like the first day of fall, I hope this Wednesday has proceeded swimmingly. Perhaps I should say, as swimmingly as 2020 can be. The crises we face seem to compound at every turn as structures, institutions, and leadership, fail regularly. However, like Howard Beale, I don’t have to tell you things are bad or to be mad.  

I will keep trying to advocate on behalf of and support the amorphous collective known as community and keep you in the loop as best I can. Part of that accounts for a compulsion to send a newsletter every weekday. However, a quick and easy way to help our community and beyond is to make sure you are registered to vote and complete the census. If you have time, maybe help people register to vote by directing them to this excellent resource from the League of Women Voters regardless of the State in which they live. 

With that, I’ll wish you the best for the rest of Wednesday; remind you that we have some meetings coming up, and I think you should check out the items below. 

Lastly, and it may be cold comfort, but it stuck in my head today, and it’s given me a bit of hope. Recently a biographer of James Baldwin was asked if Baldwin himself thought America would ever become a multi-racial democracy. The biographer responded by paraphrasing Seneca the Younger and said, “Wherever human beings are, we have a chance.”

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Where we've been, determining where we go
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: As I've mentioned, the COVID-19 trends have been going in a favorable direction around here, but we can't rest easy. For example, just today, the city announced upticks in 6 neighborhoods across the city, three of which are in Brooklyn.
item.content:encoded:
As I've mentioned, the COVID-19 trends have been going in a favorable direction around here, but we can't rest easy. For example, just today, the city announced upticks in 6 neighborhoods across the city, three of which are in Brooklyn. 

So not only remember to keep your distance and wear a mask, but also keep in mind that what we went through was the “largest mass fatality incident” in the modern history of New York City, and we don't want to go through it again. For context, last year, at this point, the city had reported a total of 30,964 deaths, while that number has more than doubled to 65,712 reported deaths, with over 20 thousand deaths to be caused by COVID-19 in 2020. It's prudent, not pessimistic, to remind folks that we’re still in the middle of this and to remain cautious.

On the positive front, you can help save democracy right here in Brooklyn by registering to vote, making a plan to vote, or becoming a poll worker. I’m biased, but if you live in the 52nd assembly district, I’d recommend signing up to be assigned in the district. Thank you to incoming Democratic district leader Jessie Pierce for setting up this form here.

You can also help save the city by filling out the census in the final eight days.

With that I’d recommend checking out the items below and hope that you enjoy the rest of your Tuesday and may fall be the best season yet.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: First, More, Last
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well. I also hope the in-person learning for 3k, Pre- K, and District 75 students, teachers, staff, and parents goes safely and smoothly.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well. I also hope the in-person learning for 3k, Pre- K, and District 75 students, teachers, staff, and parents goes safely and smoothly. The same hope extends to everyone learning remotely and for everyone kicking off 5781.

It’s the last day of summer and the first day of school for some, but since Friday, it's certainly felt like more of the same chaos and crisis that has come to define 2020. I'm referring to the passing of Brooklyn’s own Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. 

I don't know of a more significant gap on the scale of binding power than that between a Community Board to the Supreme Court. However, none of our institutions exist in a vacuum, and if you want to effect change, or even to maintain the status quo, you have to use every lever of power you have at hand. For most of us, the easiest and most direct way to do that is register to vote, or register someone else to vote even if that is a friend or relative in another state. Another simple way is to fill out the census or help someone fill out the census or become a poll worker for the upcoming election. You may also reach out to CB6 resident and the United States Senator Schumer and let his office know what you think should be done regarding the court's vacancy since he says everything is on the table.

With that, I'll say goodbye for today and recommend you check out the items below my email signature.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well as we head into the official final weekend of summer. Before getting into anything else, for all those celebrating Rosh Hashanah, I wish you L'shanah tovah. 

You may have noticed the late Brooklyn born Howard Zinn has been “trending” since the head of our Federal Executive Branch decided to issue an executive order to“ promote patriotic education.” For that reason I’ll remind everyone that Howard Zinn said, “you can’t be neutral on a moving train, ”. So, if you don't like our current direction, or want it to accelerate in the same direction, register to vote, fill out the census and help others do it. It doesn’t take much time, but these things have consequences.

Another way to avoid neutrality is to attend some of our upcoming meetings, such as October 5th’s Economic, Waterfront, Community Development & Housing Committee meeting, or October 14th’s general board meeting. The agendas and registration links are in formation, and I’ll send them out ASAP, but for now, you can mark your calendar.

There is more information below my email signature, like the ever-changing school calendar and a recap of some ranting, so I won’t keep haranguing you and let you check it out further. Enjoy the weekend and, if it applies, the rest of 5780.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: Delay, Turn, Count
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: As always, I hope this email finds you well, and thank you to everyone who caught my incorrect use of “tail” in the “tale of two cities.” Before going any further, I‘d like to thank the Warren Street tenant association for having me…
item.content:encoded:
As always, I hope this email finds you well, and thank you to everyone who caught my incorrect use of “tail” in the “tale of two cities.” Before going any further, I‘d like to thank the Warren Street tenant association for having me oversee the nominations for their elections last night, and I look forward to the candidate forum next Wednesday. 

First, as I’m sure many of you have heard, the Mayor has decided to delay in school learning for over 90% of public school students, which was supposed to begin this coming Monday. While this seems to be the correct decision, it should’ve been made, at the very least, weeks ago. It’s another example of the administration insisting something isn’t happening until the last second and forcing over a million people to turn on a dime. 

Since the spring, we’ve been making the case that school buildings shouldn’t be open for in-person learning until every safety precaution is in place. But regardless of what one thinks our position on school reopening, I can’t imagine anyone thinks plans should be announced abruptly via a press conference with no warnings to anyone, as far as I know, outside of the Tweed Courthouse or City Hall. As Assemblymember Simon noted, this will increase “massive confusion” and not only does it not help, it will “disadvantage those intended to help the most more acutely. 

There is more information on this below my email signature, so I won’t keep ranting, but I recommend checking it out. No matter what you choose, enjoy the rest of your Thursday. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Less Live, More Inequity
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: On our path to ”normalcy,” or more accurately, new normal, citywide public schools had their first day of remote learning for all students. The DOE is still issuing new guidelines while reducing the amount of live (live via remote)…
item.content:encoded:
On our path to ”normalcy,” or more accurately, new normal, citywide public schools had their first day of remote learning for all students.  The DOE is still issuing new guidelines while reducing the amount of live (live via remote) instruction students are guaranteed. The change could lead to a situation where some students receive zero live instruction on four out of five school days each week and instead rely on assignments and pre-recorded lessons posted by their teachers. This will deepen inequities in a system that’s already inequitable. 

It will be sad if this becomes the legacy of someone who became mayor talking about the “tail of 2 cities”. Does he view inequality as a feature or a flaw? As an FYI, a school in a neighboring district is shut down due to COVID-19 infections before a single student has been in the building.

Moving on, I’d like to thank all the teachers that reached out after yesterday’s newsletter and to thank them again for their service to our city.

Lastly, I hope everyone stays safe, considers reading the items below, and enjoys the evening.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well on this autumnal Tuesday. Embracing fall stereotypes, I look forward to being resplendent in plaid and sweaters. 

Putting aside fall fashion humor, I’ll be brief as a lot of people are busy with tomorrow’s first day of remote school for ALL NYC Public School students, whether they are enrolled in a blended or full remote learning option. The Mayor predicts that Covid-19 cases will be a “temporary” reality for schools this year, but I understand how some are skeptical of that claim. We are aware of how contagious this virus is, and we know 19 school employees recently tested positive, and 79 have previously died from it.

On that note, please refrain from emailing me sickening statements about teachers, and consider using your time more constructively. I have the greatest respect for teachers, and that isn't going to change.

Anyway, back to my typical optimistic wishes that you have a great Tuesday and request that you check the items below my signature.

Lastly, I hope everyone, from students’ parents, teachers, paraprofessionals, school administrators, and everyone who has worked so hard throughout the pandemic, such as District 15’s Superintendent Anita Skop and her Deputy Kelly McGuire, has a great first day of school tomorrow! 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: Simon, Schumer, Scotto
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I’d like to begin by thanking Assemblymember Simon for co-hosting a roundtable event with United States Senator and CB6 resident, Chuck Schumer. It was a small group, as it has to be, but it was none the less great to hear and so many…
item.content:encoded:
I’d like to begin by thanking Assemblymember Simon for co-hosting a roundtable event with United States Senator and CB6 resident, Chuck Schumer. It was a small group, as it has to be, but it was none the less great to hear and so many active, civically engaged voices coming out of familiar faces. They included our own Eric McClure, NYCHA Gowanus Tennant Association President Ed Tyree, Joe Rydell of the Park Slope Civic Council, among others. Everyone was masked and remains somewhat hopeful that Senator Schumer and his colleagues will push the senate majority to pass necessary aid to cities and states. 

Speaking of civic leaders, CB6 member, and 572 Warren Street resident, Joe Anne Brown, is why a young man survived a horrible fire yesterday. FDNY didn’t know that there was a young nonverbal man with special needs in danger until Joe Anne alerted them to this young man, and they turned back and rescued him. We are fortunate to have such engagement and heroism that makes you feel a little bit better about humans. So a big thank you to Joe Anne and the FDNY. 

Speaking of thanks, as I mentioned on Friday, our community mourns the loss of Salvatore ”Buddy " Scotto, who passed away at 91 years of age. Mayor de Blasio discussed Buddy's contribution to our district and the city in his press conference today. For those that want to join in remembering him, a Memorial Mass in tribute to Salvatore "Buddy" Scotto will be held in Carroll Gardens on Saturday, November 7th at Noon at Sacred Hearts - St. Stephen Church, 125 Summit Street.

With that, I’ll close and wish you the best for the remainder of the day and recommend checking out the items below my signature.  

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Remembrance & Loss
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: We all have solemn remembrances of that which was lost in life and innocence on this the 19th anniversary of the September 11th attacks that brought down the twin towers, scarred the Pentagon, and brought down a jet full of men, women, and…
item.content:encoded:
We all have solemn remembrances of that which was lost in life and innocence on this the 19th anniversary of the September 11th attacks that brought down the twin towers, scarred the Pentagon, and brought down a jet full of men, women, and children. I, the CB6 staff, and all of our members offer our deepest condolences and sympathy for those lost lives and to their loved ones who grieve that loss from that Tuesday in 2001.

Unfortunately, I have to share the sad news of Salvatore "Buddy" Scotto’s passing. A larger than life neighborhood leader and unofficial Mayor of Carroll Gardens who could never be ignored. At a time when many were leaving Brooklyn, including our cherished “South Brooklyn,” he stayed and started civic, neighborhood, and political organizations that exist to this day. Once upon a time, he was even a community board member.

He will be honored and remembered by people with far more stature than me, but I’m proud to have known him. There are many reading this message right now that I would’ve never met had it not been for Buddy. I offer my deepest condolences to his family, including his daughter CB6 member Debra Scotto.

Moving to last night’s Landmark/ Land Use meeting, which dealt with a topic that was always on Buddy's mind - that being the remediation and development of the Gowanus Canal. As advertised, our Landmark/ Land Use meeting, featured a presentation from Gowanus Lands on a park proposal to replace the current proposal for affordable housing, a park, and a school for the city-owned site commonly referred to as “public place.” Buddy told us of his involvement in getting that designation to keep the land from being alienated. You can watch the meeting here on YouTube and see the presentation slides here. I'd like to offer a big thank you to Mac Thayer for making the presentation and all the work that went into it.

We had an excellent turnout and are in the process of upgrading to be able to accommodate more folks at upcoming meetings. I should have a definite announcement this coming Monday.

As always, as we head into the weekend and keep our distance, there are lots of things happening in our community that you can check out below my signature. But before you do that, I’d recommend taking note of the fact people at 16 separate city schools have tested positive for COVID -19. Tracing is taking place to, hopefully, limit the spread.

On that note, I wish you a good and safe weekend.

Related tools

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Just like every other day, even on days that I don’t send a newsletter, I hope this message finds you well.
item.content:encoded:
Just like every other day, even on days that I don’t send a newsletter, I hope this message finds you well.

I have a few items to go over before suggesting you check out items below my signature.

Today, September 10th was supposed to be the first day of in-person learning. Unfortunately, even though the in-person start of school was moved back to September 21st and no students have attended classes in the buildings, we’ve already got two local schools (MS 88& PS 1) shut down for at least the next two weeks. Of course, there is still time to avoid an inequitable super spreader event in our schools but that’s up to a former CB6 resident.

In contrast with an event that was supposed to happen, our Landmarks/ Land Use Committee meeting is still on for 6 PM this evening. As mentioned in prior updates it will feature, along with two landmark items, a presentation from Gowanus Lands on a park proposal to replace the current proposal for affordable housing, a park, and a school for the city-owned site commonly referred to as “public place.” Register for it here and if you won’t be part of the meeting, but want to say something about it feel free to email.

With that I’ll say that there are some exciting things that you can find out about below my signature, including tonight’s F train forum and that indoor restaurant dining is set to resume on September 30th. Of course, in whatever manner you spend it, enjoy the rest of the day and stay safe.

item.title: Whole, Week, Warren
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: “You're worth the whole damn bunch put together." is the last thing Nick Caraway says to Gatsby as the summer ends out on West Egg. As summer ends here in Brooklyn, the inverse seems to be true of 2020.
item.content:encoded:
“You're worth the whole damn bunch put together." is the last thing Nick Caraway says to Gatsby as the summer ends out on West Egg. As summer ends here in Brooklyn, the inverse seems to be true of 2020. However, the earth keeps spinning, the sun rises, and the planet has an estimated 5 billion years left. Give or take a millennium.

With all that in mind, we attempt to persevere in the face of a new normal. We meet via Zoom and other distance keeping measures. For instance, on Thursday, the CB6 landmarks/ land use committee has a virtual meeting. It starts at 6 pm; you register for it here, and it will feature, along with two landmark items, a presentation from Gowanus Lands on a park proposal for the city-owned site commonly referred to as “public place.” 

Next, I’d like to thank the Warren Street Tenants Association for inviting me to their meeting Friday night. I also thank them for trusting me to help oversee their tenant elections this fall. It’s a great honor to be asked, and I am excited to do it. 

As usual, I recommend reading below my signature, completing the census, enjoying the rest of your day, and may the next four months of this infamous year be worth far more than the prior eight put together.

item.title: Happy Labor Day
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Also, from the Department of Education, the 2020-2021 school year calendar is now available. As previously announced, remote learning will start on September 16 with a transitional period.
item.content:encoded:
Also, from the Department of Education, the 2020-2021 school year calendar is now available. As previously announced, remote learning will start on September 16 with a transitional period. September 21 is the first full day of school, with blended learning beginning on that day. Unlike in previous years, students will have a full day of school remotely on Election Day. The last day of school is scheduled for June 25. All breaks and holidays from the previous academic year remain as before except for the April break. The April break will be one week long, two days shorter than scheduled for last April.

The only labor I recommend on Labor Day, if you haven’t already done it, is dedicating 10 minutes of work and fill out the census as there are only 23 days left to do so.

On a final note, I wish you, a restful Labor Day; suggest checking out the items below my signature and hope you stay safe.

item.content:encoded:
As you may have noticed in yesterday's newsletter, the next Landmarks/Land Use meeting includes a presentation on a proposal for an alternative use exclusively as a park at the site commonly referred to as Public Place, along with two landmarking items. It'll take place via zoom, and you can join the meeting when it begins at 6 PM. Speaking of Gowanus, there's coverage in City Limits of the debate around the timing of the pending rezoning proposal. Keep in mind that we were on the record before the coronavirus made social distancing a thing asking for extensive pre-certification/ULURP review.

I'm sure you'll be hearing more about Gowanus as the calendar moves forward, and I'll certainly keep you posted, but in the meantime, check out the items below my email signature and please help increase our census completion numbers.

Before closing, I'd be remiss if I didn't acknowledge the loss of and pay tribute to the greatest of the few NY Mets baseball legends, Tom Seaver. He is among the growing number of those with comorbidities who we've lost to COVID-19. I'm not qualified to write his full obituary. Still, I always admired "Tom Terrific's" willingness to publicly state his opposition to the Vietnam War, saying that "if the Mets can win the World Series, then we can get out of Vietnam."

It's still helpful to remember what is possible, especially these days.

item.title: Delay, Spray, Save
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well on this first Wednesday of September, and as the unofficial end of summer draws closer.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well on this first Wednesday of September, and as the unofficial end of summer draws closer.

I assume you know that public school buildings remain closed and in-person learning has been delayed for at least 11 days. School openings now are to start on September 21st. A lot of people are not pleased with, what is again, a plan that seems to be made, and adjusted on the fly. Still, at least it was an acknowledgment that we don’t have to rush 1.1 million children back into schools with unnecessary risk and a guaranteed spike in virus cases. I’ve noticed, as a way to counter such caution, some people are claiming that only 6 percent of the over 180,000 COVID-19 deaths are death attributable to the virus and thus an acceptable fact of life. If it’s not dishonest it is, at best, void of empathy.

We have a lot of stuff happening around the district, like spraying for mosquitoes and more that you can check out by reading past my email signature. But before doing that, I’ll remind you that a school delay doesn’t mean anything if the necessary safety improvements aren’t made. So, if you have thoughts on this, regardless of what they are, or if you want to make sure literacy teachers aren’t roving substitutes, feel free to submit testimony in advance of tomorrow’s city council education committee.

On that note, I wish you all the best and will have some exciting announcements over the next couple of days.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.content:encoded:
First, as mentioned yesterday, there is the District 15 Rally & March for Safe Schools beginning at 11:30 in Cobble Hill Park and marching up to 5th Avenue then ending in Sunset Park. Also mentioned yesterday, you may send a letter to city elected officials asking them to keep literacy teachers in place to use their effective expertise to advance literacy instead of being used as a scattered group of substitute teachers. It takes less than a minute, and you'll be joining us in the company of Assemblymembers Simon & Carroll, Councilmember Lander, Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, and over 600 others who have already shown their support for ULIT.

One last thing on the school front is the City Council's Education Committee hearing on Thursday at 10:00 AM, considering a resolution asking to delay school building reopening's until buildings are made safe for all. You can register to testify or submit testimony here.

Anyway, I'll stop here and recommend checking out the items below, such as gyms reopening tomorrow and a reminder that we are down to 29 days left to complete the census. The census is so easy and so important to complete. It takes under 10 minutes and can help stop us from losing more congressional seats added to the prior loss of 40% of our seats due to undercounting over the course of the last seven censuses.

On that note, no matter what you do with the rest of it, enjoy the first day of September.

Best,

item.title: Literacy & Letters
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: It seems that, on an almost weekly basis, the New York Times is publishing yet another premature obituary for our city with misleading headlines, contradictory statements, and suburban real estate interests as primary sources. Anyway, I…
item.content:encoded:
It seems that, on an almost weekly basis, the New York Times is publishing yet another premature obituary for our city with misleading headlines, contradictory statements, and suburban real estate interests as primary sources. Anyway, I find it repulsive, and it brings me to the brink of canceling my Times subscription.

Anyway, in Friday's newsletter, or elsewhere, you may have noticed an article about the possible redeployment of literacy teachers across the city as smaller class sizes tell a tale of staffing shortages. The article featured Assemblymember Jo Anne Simon's letter to Education Chancellor Carranza highlighting the importance of literacy, the effectiveness of teachers dedicated to literacy, and what a mistake it would be to have such teachers reassigned to roles unrelated literacy. I spoke with Assemblymember on Friday and thanked her for her dedication to this matter, and with it, we've also sent a letter indicating our shared sentiments.

Efforts to ensure literacy teachers and coaches remain in their current roles are based on the conclusion that, as our letter states, "the upcoming school year will require even greater assistance for everyone involved in helping students gain literacy skills." Besides that reality, the Department of Education's own study indicates schools that have ULIT coaches in them have seen reading comprehension metrics improve by over 20 percent. Difficult times put a premium on setting the right priorities.

If you want to be in the great company of Assemblymember Simon and CB6, you can take a minute (literally) and join this letter-writing campaign organized by literacy teachers. You can also submit testimony and let your thoughts be known at the virtual City Council education meeting on Thursday morning.

Whether you agree with me or not, I wish you all the best for the rest of August and recommend checking out the items below my email signature.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Learning, Funding, Planning
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: As always, some interesting stuff is happening across our district. Including the final night of “Dine in Park Slope,” art walks in Gowanus and Red Hook, bluegrass on the canal, or a BBQ celebrating the Census with our friends at Red Hook…
item.content:encoded:
As always, some interesting stuff is happening across our district. Including the final night of “Dine in Park Slope,” art walks in Gowanus and Red Hook, bluegrass on the canal, or a BBQ celebrating the Census with our friends at Red Hook Initiative. 

Speaking of the census, if you haven’t done so already or missed Assemblymember Jo Anne Simon & CB6 member Jason Reischel at Whole Foods, take 10 minutes, click here and fill it out. It will help our community, borough, and city receive the federal funding and representation it deserves. As shown during our current crisis, such funding is necessary to help avoid mass layoffs, government services such as trains and buses. 

Obviously I have a bias towards helping New York, but it’s not in New York’s interest; it’s in the countries. Take, for example, that New York City’s population is less than 3% percent of the country, less than 1% of its landmass. At the same time, NYC produces nearly 10% of it’s Gross Domestic Product(GDP) while receiving billions less from the federal government than it pays out through taxes. We are fortunate that our federal reps are fighting and already voted to make this happen, but making that funding appear, requires the other branches of the legislative to process to take action. 

While that may not be in the city’s control, one thing that the city does control is how, and when, our public schools reopen. Just like earlier in the week, it seems like unless a noted fitness enthusiast from Park Slope changes course or a thousand schools that had ventilation problems as of yesterday are instantly safe, we’re headed for a school strike. As I’ve said I’ll share it immediately if I get any more information on this. 

Anyway, I’ll stop here, suggest seeing past my signature, and have a great weekend. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well on this humid Thursday as educational events commemorating the Battle of Brooklyn are offered virtually by our friends at the Old Stone House.

Speaking of education, there seems to be confusion about the difference between a strike and a boycott among many journalists. On the subject of learning, there is a growing consensus that we shouldn’t begin doing so in school buildings until they are safe for all. item.title: Suggesting, Lacking, Needing
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: As announced yesterday, the Mayor has given schools the go-ahead for outdoor learning. I don’t mean to be brief in my description, but that does fully describe it.
item.content:encoded:
As announced yesterday, the Mayor has given schools the go-ahead for outdoor learning. I don’t mean to be brief in my description, but that does fully describe it.

It was given the go-ahead just ten days after schools were required to submit their hybrid learning plans to the Department of Education (DOE). Those plans had to detail student capacity, which now is likely to shift again.

Outdoor learning is, rightly, seen as a good idea on its own. However, the context in which it was announced and under which it will be implemented is opaque, especially if one cares about educational equity.

Areas with the highest infection rates are ostensibly given priority, but those are also the areas lacking in resources, and PTA funding. Chancellor Carranza suggested that well-heeled PTAs could, but are not compelled, to make up gaps for those less endowed. The Mayor hasn’t provided an estimate of how much this could cost. A suggestion is hardly a guarantee when it comes to health and finances- especially when the city continues to have an unemployment rate above 20%.

Yet again, this highlights the need for federal aid and absent such help state assistance. If anyone receiving this email is one of his major donors, please feel free to share it with our Governor.

Anyway, I’ll stop there and remind you that there are less than 40 days to complete the census, recommend that you check out the items below my signature, including tonight’s NYCHA town hall and Thursday’s “Java with Jo Anne”.

No matter what, enjoy the rest of your Tuesday.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Coffee, Canal, Cleaning
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Public Schools and the city’s plan, or lack thereof, remains the focus of literally, with there being 1.1 million students along with their parents, guardians, teachers, and staff, millions of people.
item.content:encoded:
Public Schools and the city’s plan, or lack thereof, remains the focus of literally, with there being 1.1 million students along with their parents, guardians, teachers, and staff, millions of people.

In case it wasn’t clear already, you can add City Council Speaker Johnson and NYC Comptroller Scott Scott Stringer to the list of those calling for a delayed reopening of schools, and questioning the timing and real commitment to a "plan" for outdoor learning. Let’s not forget where we were, as we try but aren’t always ahead of the curve on this matter. You’d be hard-pressed to find officials outside the administration who would agree with the Mayor in declaring that this will be the “safest school year ever.” Even if all were to go reasonably well, this is an impossible and bizarre statement.

I hope you rise above these difficult times and enjoy the rest of the day. Please check out the items below my email signature, and have a remote cup of “Java with Jo Anne” tomorrow morning and read about the growing list of ways the Gowanus Dredgers bring the community together.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: Outdoors, Equity, Seinfeld
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: For some, it may seem like yesterday that we were first hearing terms like "socially distanced" and "remote learning." On the learning front, it has been 164 days since schools closed back in March, and now just two weeks before their…
item.content:encoded:
For some, it may seem like yesterday that we were first hearing terms like "socially distanced" and "remote learning." On the learning front, it has been 164 days since schools closed back in March, and now just two weeks before their scheduled reopening, the Mayor has unveiled an "outdoor learning plan." Schools have until Friday to submit plans for outdoor space, and it's, at best, unclear how they'll obtain resources like tents.

For access to outdoor learning to be equitable, significant additional resources must be given to many schools. We can't just rely on PTA's with adequate resources to then share with other schools. Real and direct support is needed from all levels of government, but it is federal assistance that is most sorely needed.

Schools and equity within them have been a hot topic of late, and if you want to support a school in our district on these matters, consider reading and then signing this petition. We have written a letter to this effect as well. By signing this petition, you'd be joining many CB6 members along with notable signatories such as Assemblymember Jo Anne Simon, Councilmember Carlos Menchaca, former Assemblymember Joan Millman, Senator-elect Jabari Brisport, Assemblymember- elect Marcela Mitaynes, District Leader- elect Jesse Pierce and Public Advocate Jumaane Williams. As I've said before, I don't think anyone wants the already profound impact of COVID-19 to be compounded by an increase in inequity in education.

Another outdoor-related item relates to our restaurants that can use your help to survive. If you can afford to, please support our local businesses, and don't forget that "Dine in Park Slope" is going on until Friday! 

With that, I’ll recommend reading further but either way I hope you enjoy the rest of your Monday.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Not Unto
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: It's been great to engage in clarifying conversations with people who have responded so thoughtfully and passionately with varying perspectives regarding school building and in-person learning. This past week I have been raising the issue…
item.content:encoded:
It's been great to engage in clarifying conversations with people who have responded so thoughtfully and passionately with varying perspectives regarding school building and in-person learning. This past week I have been raising the issue of Sunset Park school building reopening's and in-person learning in light of its high COVID-19 positive testing rate (7%) compared to the city average of below 1%.

I have been asked why this focus since it's outside of CB6? While we may be a city of islands (except for the Bronx), no community in our city is an island unto itself, and anyway, Sunset Park is part of the same school district. It does not exist in isolation.

Children travel within the school district (especially middle schoolers) and throughout the city (especially high schoolers). Plus, this is a significant equity issue, and we don't want the already profound impact of COVID-19 to increase inequity in education when it can be prevented.

With that, I'll wish you all the best this weekend while still suggesting that you scroll down for more information, such as news on absentee voting and things to do, which appear below my email signature.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Building Equity, Average Metaphor
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I begin by thanking everyone for their responses to yesterday’s newsletter and specifically our letter indicating support for a delay of in-person school reopening in solidarity with District 15 principals, many parents, and teachers on…
item.content:encoded:
I begin by thanking everyone for their responses to yesterday’s newsletter and specifically our letter indicating support for a delay of in-person school reopening in solidarity with District 15 principals, many parents, and teachers on behalf of our students. I am making my way through the many comments as quickly as I can.

Some points deserve further clarification. First, the COVID-19 testing average, while undoubtedly and thankfully low is still only an average and not reflective of specific circumstances within our communities. For example, within School District 15, we have some areas testing 0 percent while in Sunset Park the rate has has regularly been as high as 7% with testing that some feel isn’t nearly enough. With an across the board 3% citywide threshold to close school buildings we face a situation in which the extra burdens on some communities are exacerbated with dire consequences. If you agree and would like to support a delay in reopening, the Equity Team, at PS 169, has written this letter and petition you can sign on to by clicking here.

To use a metaphor, if Bill Gates walks into a bar (not the start of a joke), the average net worth of those in the bar would be in the billions, but only one would be a billionaire. Applying this to a highly contagious virus in places with poor ventilation and cuts to funding (as is the case with schools) and you’re going to further raise the level of infection, an infection that we know rapidly spreads. We can't pretend it's going to stay isolated in one community and will we then see schools again closing down. Isn't it better to heed principals, and others in charge of their schools expressing concerns for all their students and staff and wait until we have appropriate protections in place? 

This is not just a hypothetical. It is drawing from a clear trend in education in which schools have tried unsuccessfully to reopen for in-person learning. Even here in Brooklyn, among communities that were thought to be nearing herd immunity, spikes continue to occur after single events.

To be clear, I don't know of anyone (unless they became owners of Zoom this past January) who wants remote learning and other such systems to become the norm. However, unfortunately, until in-person education is safe online learning is going to be a part of life.

Now back to our regularly scheduled items below my signature and a wish that you enjoy the rest of your Thursday. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: A Battle, A Letter, A Percentage
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Dedicated readers of this newsletter will take note of 2 consistent themes of late. One is the dedication of New Yorkers in following COVID-19 safety protocols, and the other is concern about the reopening of school buildings this…
item.content:encoded:
Dedicated readers of this newsletter will take note of 2 consistent themes of late. One is the dedication of New Yorkers in following COVID-19 safety protocols, and the other is concern about the reopening of school buildings this September.

Regarding the former, the city reported its lowest positive test percentage (0.24%) since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Let's not forget that while that is a great number, it doesn't speak for all communities and keeping it that low, and lower, requires that we don't let up on safety.

One mistake would be to ignore the calls of our School District 15 principals, teachers, and families that have made clear that schools should not reopen in September. They together with the UFT have asked for a delay and phase-in of in-person learning this fall. For that reason, we have sent a letter to the Mayor and Chancellor supporting The delay in in-person instruction until adequate plans have been made and implemented for safety.

There are more items related to schools and various other happenings listed below my email signature that I suggest you check out. I hope you enjoy the rest of your day. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Dedication, Distance, Testing
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: New Yorkers' dedication to following safety protocols has overcome health experts who thought our numbers would be rising again . Instead we steadily remain just below a 1% infection rate.
item.content:encoded:
New Yorkers' dedication to following safety protocols has overcome health experts who thought our numbers would be rising again . Instead we steadily remain just below a 1% infection rate. Of course, we have to keep in mind that it’s not 1% everywhere, and it’s much higher in communities neighboring CB6, such as Sunset Park.

We can’t just be dedicated to safety for ourselves, but we have to ensure that everyone we share our city with is safe, and we should adopt policies reflecting that. I’ll make the point again that our prior statements on schools, and the eventual return to school buildings, wasn’t posturing or shouting at the wind. Wanting schools open doesn’t mean that safety can be ignored for the most vulnerable. Safety must be ensured FOR EVERYONE.

As of now, especially as schools that tried to open are returning to all remote,  it doesn’t seem like the physical plant of schools and degree of preparation can be overcome by even the most well intentioned attempts at distancing. Having closed too slowly is not an argument for opening too quickly.

On that note, I’ll recommend reading on down and hope that you enjoy the rest of your Tuesday.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Dine, MEND, Workout
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Throughout this pandemic, the issue of small businesses has been, whether through macro-scale policy and assistance, locally organized support or questions of how to reopen, a big one. Of course, we want them to remain as part of our city…
item.content:encoded:
Throughout this pandemic, the issue of small businesses has been, whether through macro-scale policy and assistance, locally organized support or questions of how to reopen, a big one. Of course, we want them to remain as part of our city and community and be good and prosperous neighbors. 

The city’s Office of Nightlife took a step in that direction with the announcement of the MEND initiative(Mediating Establishment and Neighbor Disputes) which will work to resolve quality of life issues in our community and across the city. Given my experience as a former chair of our permits and licenses committee, before not only having been superseded but surpassed by the current chair, Rachel Freeman, I know having a localized office to deal with such issues is excellent. If it works as intended, it’ll be mutually beneficial to improve the quality of life for neighbors while potentially reducing violations and fines at a time when businesses can least afford them.

I am not alone, I spoke to former councilman Rafael Espinal whose legislation created this office, and he made clear that the goal is to create a space where communities and nightlife can resolve issues without the need for police or enforcement agency involvement. I’m excited and hopeful that this will fulfill its promise. 

Speaking of helping small businesses check out “Dine in PARK Slope,” which starts tonight and runs through August 28th. Thank you to all of those who worked to organize and maintain this annual tradition. Kudos the Park Slope 5th Avenue and the North Flatbush BIDs.

To work up, an appetite read the items below and enjoy the rest of your Monday.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org
