item.title: Too Fast, Bowling, Museums & More
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: A major topic these days, as COVID-19 positive testing rates have remained around 1%, is how we get back to any semblance of normalcy without it leading to a spike in cases. One of the most significant components of that return is, of…
item.content:encoded:
A major topic these days, as COVID-19 positive testing rates have remained around 1%, is how we get back to any semblance of normalcy without it leading to a spike in cases. One of the most significant components of that return is, of course, reopening schools. 

Before the Mayor closed the schools, we said they should be closed, later on, during the pandemic, we said that schools shouldn’t open, and school staff and students shouldn't go back into school buildings until every safety protocol is put in place. Part of that safety, along with the PPE, is keeping the infection rate low. While the rates in much of CB6 are low, the same can’t be said in neighboring communities such as Sunset Park. Sunset Park has seen a spike, and infection rates are around 7% percent, which is more than double the threshold that would require the schools to close.

We need to have plans and protocols to better adjust to specific needs in our local communities and everyone, no matter if you have kids or not, should be concerned that necessary steps and precautions aren't being taken now. The city at the beginning closed down schools too late; we shouldn’t reopen them too quickly. 

This perspective is broadly shared by teachers, principals, and families alike. 

Speaking of principals, I want to wish all the best to M.S. 51 Principal Lenore Berner on her retirement and welcome acting Principal Neal Singh to the community. 

I leave you with my regular suggestion to read on and get some ideas and information or a recap the week. In any event, stay safe and have a great weekend. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Collegial, Community, Questions
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I don’t have a ton to say besides the listings below my email signature but to shout out, in light of the spike of COVID-19 cases in Sunset Park, that we must remain vigilant about safety protocols- keep our distance, cover our noses and…
item.content:encoded:
I don’t have a ton to say besides the listings below my email signature but to shout out, in light of the spike of COVID-19 cases in Sunset Park, that we must remain vigilant about safety protocols- keep our distance, cover our noses and mouths and sanitize, sanitize, sanitize.

I recommend checking out this piece from my counterpart at the Bronx Community Board 6, District Manager John Sanchez, which highlights some fundamental questions. Questions like, what obligation, when it comes to affordable housing, does the entire city have to a district like his that suffers from a 31% poverty rate and a 30% unemployment rate?

These questions, and how we answer them are always important, but especially when tough choices must be made and priorities among policies must be set. We are being tested. In 2014 our board was the only Community Board in Brooklyn to agree with our legislature to approve Mandatory Inclusionary Housing. Do we stand by principle when it comes to practice or were we just paying lip service?

Of course, we must always look at details and context of various approaches and plans to craft approvals, caveats, or disapprovals . As my colleague suggests we live not only in a community but a city, state, and country.

No matter your answers, I hope you stay safe and enjoy the rest of your Thursday.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Staying inside to keep cool? It's the perfect time to fill out the census if you haven't yet done so.
item.content:encoded:
Staying inside to keep cool? It's the perfect time to fill out the census if you haven't yet done so. I recommend using the very device you’re reading on, invest about 10 minutes and get yourself counted so we, as a state and city, get the resources and representation we need and deserve from the federal government. It is a guaranteed return on that investment.

There are some interesting things happening today both outside and in our virtual reality.

An important one is an information session hosted by the Department of Education about the upcoming school year that concerns everyone. That’s not just parents, students, and teachers but as this letter makes clear, principals across District 15 are raising concerns about logistical safety.

Relax and read the rest of this email to discover something useful. Most importantly, keep cool, stay safe, and enjoy the rest of your day.

item.title: Good Going Forward
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well on this eleventh day of the eighth month of the year two thousand and twenty.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well on this eleventh day of the eighth month of the year two thousand and twenty.

A big thank you to everyone who responded to my takedown of the myth of a less infectious, and therefore safer, suburbia. It always feels good to be reminded you’re not the only one who loves living in our city, borough, and community.

That doesn’t mean that the city is at its best. Objectively bad things still abound. However, good things are happening in CB6, almost daily, and you'll find them in the updates below my signature.

Speaking of good things happening in CB6, I had lunch with the 25th state senate district’s new occupant in the coming term, Jabari Brisport (he is running unopposed). The district includes parts of the CB6 neighborhoods of Gowanus, Red Hook, Carroll Gardens and Park Slope. I left confident that we’ll have a fighter for tenants, safe streets, a safe environment, and more. Expanding my horizons, the senator-elect introduced me to an excellent vegan burger- a description I would’ve previously thought to be oxymoronic. He, of course, has big shoes to fill as he succeeds retiring State Senator Velmanette Montgomery.

Anyway, I'm sure we’ll be hearing more from Jabari in the coming months and years, in the meantime stay safe and cool, check out the items below my signature, and enjoy the rest of your Tuesday. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Surveys, Schools, Reminders
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: In this weather, nobody wants to read ramblings, so I’ll be brief. There is a heat advisory that will begin today at noon and be in effect until Wednesday evening.
item.content:encoded:
In this weather, nobody wants to read ramblings, so I’ll be brief. There is a heat advisory that will begin today at noon and be in effect until Wednesday evening. Cooling centers will be open while still requiring social distancing protocols. Those simple protocols, keeping a safe distance & wearing masks, are what have lead us to yesterday's .78 positivity percentage, which is the lowest we’ve seen since tracking began back in March.  

Although I may be preaching to the choir, our city is getting some lousy coverage these days from places like the New York Times, which uses suburban real estate agents/ interests as their primary sources for articles telling people why they should leave the city. I think it’s important to point out that these suburbs all have a higher rate of COVID-19 cases per 100,000 people when compared to New York City. 

New York City has 2,743 cases per 100,000 residents. By comparison, also per every 100 thousand residents, the number of COVID -19 cases in Westchester is 3,732, Nassau County 3,208, Suffolk County 2,955, Orange County 2,894, and 4,272 in Rockland County.

Anyway, stay safe and cool, check out the items below my signature, and enjoy the rest of your Monday.

item.title: Loss, Anecdote, Empathy
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I’ll get into more mundane things below my signature, but I couldn’t start today without commenting on the death of the great New York writer Pete Hamill. Pete Hamill was born and raised in our community long before community boards or…
item.content:encoded:
I’ll get into more mundane things below my signature, but I couldn’t start today without commenting on the death of the great New York writer Pete Hamill. Pete Hamill was born and raised in our community long before community boards or community districts were a thing. His father worked in a Gowanus factory, and he, a high school dropout, became a powerful voice in our city. No one is perfect, but he is right up there in the annals of tabloid journalism with Jimmy Breslin. We’d be well served to remember his love for the city; it’s constant change and diversity expressed in most of his writing. 

I only got to meet Pete Hamill once, but I’ll never forget. It was, fittingly, in CB6 at Red Hook's Rocky Sullivan's just after I had graduated college in 2007. He read from his then-new book North River, told stories about Brooklyn, and at one point, he discussed what a great day it was when his Italian neighbor had taught his Irish mother how to make red sauce,or ,as some would say, gravy. After this anecdote, he explained to the crowd, “some may not know this, but the Irish and Italians hated each other until they started marrying each other.” 

Being the offspring of precisely this type of marital mix (Italian father, Irish Mother), it resonated with me, and when I was introduced to him, I was able to tell him so. I’m sure countless people had told him how his words had resonated with them, but for the few minutes I got to speak with him, he gave the impression that it was a unique experience that he wouldn’t forget. Regardless, I never forgot it and will always appreciate it.

I'd guess the ability to speak to someone he didn't know with care and empathy is part of what made him so successful in various aspects of writing. No matter the field, we'd all do better with a bit more empathy, especially as there is so much human suffering around us.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Storm, Soliloquy, Safety Share this article as a link
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: New York City’s Office of Emergency Management (OEM) has issued a Tropical Storm Warning in effect citywide, with heavy rains and strong winds from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m., with the most substantial rains and tropical strength winds…
item.content:encoded:
New York City’s Office of Emergency Management (OEM) has issued a Tropical Storm Warning in effect citywide, with heavy rains and strong winds from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m., with the most substantial rains and tropical strength winds from noon to 2 p.m. Tuesday. OEM has also issued a travel advisory from this morning through tonight.  As I was preparing to send this email, a tornado warning was added to our list of things to be concerned about.

The city activated a virtual Emergency Operations Center (EOC), and it’s Flash Flood Emergency Plan has been enabled to help mitigate potential flash flooding and ensure a quick, effective, and coordinated response to any flash flood events that do occur. NYC Department of Environmental Protection, Department of Transportation, and Department of Sanitation teams are out clearing catch basins in preparation for the storm. The City has also placed the Downed Tree Task Force on alert. This multi-agency task force is responsible for coordinating the response to a significant downed tree event.

As we receive more information, our office will share it. Thank you, Assistant District Manager, Ty Beatty,for jumping on conference calls with Con Ed to check in with them as they monitor the storm.

Moving on to things still happening, virtually, outside of the storm. Public Advocate Jumaane Williams hosts a NYCHA & Health town hall with the Fifth Avenue Committee, the Gowanus Neighborhood Coalition for Justice, and others. If you haven’t already, taken part in such a meeting, check it out as it is part of our new normal. We will probably be using such formats to advance civic engagement for a long time.

Our virtual meetings have had a greater turnout than all in-person meetings combined for the prior year. A “back of the envelope” calculation shows 1,400 who’ve attended our 3 virtual meetings and 800 who’ve attended our ten general board meetings of the last year. We also had excellent turnout for our committee meeting on the state of local business.

Turnout isn’t the only argument in favor of such options. For example, there is a growing body of social science that indicates highly motivated factions not reflective of broader public opinion, can derail not just public meetings, but entire projects. A leading factor in this is due to the fact the affluent among us can more easily arrange their schedules to pack in-person meetings.

Keeping that in mind our district has a median household income of 137 thousand dollars a year and is the city’s 2nd wealthiest.

Anyway, that’s enough of a social science soliloquy for today. I hope you check out the items below but,more importantly, stay safe.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Reminder of Revenue
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I’ll begin with a practical reminder that Alternate Side Parking regulations are back in effect until September 5th. I’m guessing this is because the Mayor read our letter suggesting he layout month to month schedules for ASP.
item.content:encoded:
I’ll begin with a practical reminder that Alternate Side Parking regulations are back in effect until September 5th. I’m guessing this is because the Mayor read our letter suggesting he layout month to month schedules for ASP.

While we wait for, but aren't assured of federal aid , the state is looking at various policy options to close the budget gap. It’s important to note, as Governor Cuomo said last week, the money has to “ come from somewhere .” The preference is, of course, for the federal government to pass some version of the HEROES Act , owing to its ability to run necessary deficits to supply disaster relief. However, if that is not to come, closing the budget gap doesn’t have to be done on the backs of those who can least afford it.

Instead, there are legislative proposals to do so by increasing taxes on New York State's wealthiest, commonly referred to as billionaires. New York’s 118 billionaires have seen their net worth increase by $77 billion since coronavirus hit the United States. Those gains, coming in just three months, are more than five times the size of the state’s entire projected budget shortfall of $14 billion. 

While there is always the prospect that they may abandon the state, this has not happened in the past or elsewhere to any significant degree . What is this risk weighed against whether working people can afford to get to work?

Anyway, I’ll disembark from my soapbox and wish you a great Monday, and hopefully, you check out the items, including coverage of a letter we wrote , below.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201

item.title: Conserving, Speaking, Applying
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Unless you know something I don’t, I can’t imagine anyone referring to 2020 as a “typical” year. It’s involved various crises, calls for change and a search for the best of difficult ways forward.
item.content:encoded:
Unless you know something I don’t, I can’t imagine anyone referring to 2020 as a “typical” year. It’s involved various crises, calls for change and a search for the best of difficult ways forward. We’re still figuring out schools, dining out, recreation, and even a greeting as simple as a handshake is so yesterday. The path ahead is informed by our view of the moment, our values, and by previous experience. It requires serious study to arrive at acceptable answers.

For example, we already have 3,000 permanently closed businesses across the city , is there something that can be done to prevent further losses? I’ve mentioned it before, but it is worth repeating that Assemblymember Robert Carroll, has a bill that would go a long way toward stemming the tide. His bill would require insurance companies that are sitting on billions in excessive reserves to payout to their insureds on “Business Interruption Claims”. Many businesses have been paying premiums for years. How much do we value such things as independent restaurants, shops, and nonprofits as part of a post-pandemic city? 

During these contentious times, how deeply do we value freedom of speech? The organization Vocal NY which was to open a headquarters here in BKCB6, after leading protests against the recently adopted FY21 budget had their previously approved funding rescinded.

If this revocation is a matter of absolute necessity, it is understandable. However, there are serious concerns that it was done as a form of retribution for the protests . The group received the funding based on previous work they had done, and protesting doesn’t change that work and, unless we want to limit speech, it shouldn’t impact their future work. In support of that proposition, not as an evaluation of what they protested, but in support of their rights to do so, we wrote a letter to the New York City Council Speaker, Corey Johnson asking the funding to be restored.

I think it’s a safe bet that nobody wants to have the post-pandemic world be a place in which people must fall in line to continue what was acknowledged to be good works. Speaking of speech, it's a safe bet that you have heard enough from me for today, so keep scrolling down and enjoy the rest of your Thursday. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Seeking clarity on both sides of the street
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Having heard quite a bit from constituents, often in direct response to this email (from drivers and non-drivers alike) asking for greater clarity and longer-term planning for Alternate Side Parking (ASP), we highlighted such concerns to…
item.content:encoded:
Having heard quite a bit from constituents, often in direct response to this email (from drivers and non-drivers alike) asking for greater clarity and longer-term planning for Alternate Side Parking (ASP), we highlighted such concerns to those in charge .  

We know that transportation, and especially parking, is a contentious issue. Still, I think it’s safe to say there is a solid consensus that the streets should be cleaned, and if we’re going to have alternate side regulations, people should have more than a day’s notice.

As our letter states , we’ve asked the administration to develop more precise and consistent criteria for the implementation, or suspension, of Alternate Side Parking regulations to avoid, for example, announcing on a Sunday a change to take effect on Monday. Such an approach, we’d hope, would lead to more drivers parking their cars appropriately and thus accomplish the stated purpose of cleaning the streets instead of perpetuating the sight of street sweepers weaving in and out from the curb, leaving garbage and tickets in their wake,

With that, I’ll say I think you should continue reading, especially about Red Hook & NYCHA , but either way, stay cool and enjoy your Wednesday.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: Heat & Happenings
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well rested after the weekend. However, it seems as if all the days blend much like the proposed school model , in this time of COVID-19.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well rested after the weekend. However, it seems as if all the days blend much like the proposed school model , in this time of COVID-19.

One distinctive aspect of weekends nowadays is the open streets & open restaurants program that has encouraged responsible social interaction and helped businesses that had been closed for months. Parts of Park Slope and Red Hook are seeing the benefits now. Companies can find out more details and apply here.

This program not only helps now, but our post-pandemic city will be shaped by what we do while in its midst. The businesses we support, the transportation options we choose are all actions that will have a lasting impact. We can't assume our local shops will be there when we get back to “normal" if we rely exclusively on Amazon Prime now.

So, as various businesses and cultural institutions we’ve missed start to open, don’t just give thanks give them your patronage. We can also urge lawmakers at the state and federal levels, especially, to enact policies that help them stay viable.

Speaking of lawmakers, one of the best there was, a personal friend, mentor, and employer of mine, former Assemblymember Joan Millman , as many of may know, had decided not to run for re-election as female district leader for the 52nd assembly district. Following Joan in anything is a tough act, but in the Assembly, Jo Anne Simon has done a great job. So with that, I’d like to give a big congratulations to Jesse Pierce, who has been elected to succeed Joan . I'm confident she will do a great job, and I look forward to her making Brooklyn a greater democracy.

As always, there are some suggestions for things to do, see, and read below my email signature. If you check them out, great if not have a good Monday and remember alternate side parking is suspended this week.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Recapping, Reminding, Thinking, Surveying
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I begin by thanking everyone who took part in last night's “back to school “ town hall. This appreciation applies to the over 500 attendees, Department of Education(DOE) leadership, great friend to CB6, D15 Superintendent Skop Anita Skop,…
item.content:encoded:
I begin by thanking everyone who took part in last night's “back to school “ town hall. This appreciation applies to the over 500 attendees, Department of Education(DOE) leadership, great friend to CB6, D15 Superintendent Skop Anita Skop, and last but not least, Councilmember Lander and his staff (especially Naomi Dann).

It was a great meeting, and a lot of important questions were asked, and DOE did their best to answer them. However, as is the norm for 2020, and like our EWCDH meeting on Monday, a significant theme of the night was uncertainty. This goes for questions around “blended” learning, remote learning, who’d be teaching under which setting, what new training educators will have, schedules, and of course, safety. With that uncertainty, it’s even more critical that parents of public school students take the ” return to school preference” survey, which is due by August 7th.

If that paragraph doesn’t suffice or if you weren’t there or just want to rewatch the meeting, click here and to see the presentation given by the DOE’s Deputy Chancellor Adrienne Austin, which focused on programming models, click here . As we find out more about what this school year will look like, I’ll keep you posted.

For now, just know I hope you have a good weekend, and please check out the items below, including the Botany Walk and Boathouse. No matter what you decide, do it at a safe distance and wear a mask.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well on this warm Thursday in July. You too may wonder if things will ever, no matter how flat the curve , get back to a normal wouldn’t have received good grades anyway.Speaking of the abnormal and grading, what we thought of as “back to school” probably won't and shouldn't be the same unless a COVID-19 vaccine is ready sooner than even the most optimistic predictions would have it.

Tonight we hope to get some clarity about the back to school conundrum. We proudly co-sponsor a “Back To School Town Hall with Councilmember Lander . The town hall will feature leadership from the Department of Education, including Deputy Chancellor Adrienne Austin, Executive Superintendent Karen Watts, and District 15 Superintendent Anita Skop. Keep your eyes peeled, and you may notice the LinkNYC kiosks telling you it’s the place to be.

Below my signature, there are some more places to be, literally and virtually, such as the Old Stone House’s Beer & Botany walk tomorrow night . I recommend scrolling through it, note what interests you, and then remember to join the town hall this evening.

Wherever you go, keep a socially responsible distance, and cover your face, to have a regret-free Thursday.

item.title: for H LInk
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: If you read this newsletter or have met me, you know I love all things voting; the act of voting itself, reminding people to vote and registering folks to vote. Some may recall that pre-pandemic I’d tell people that if they saw me out and…
item.content:encoded:
If you read this newsletter or have met me, you know I love all things voting; the act of voting itself, reminding people to vote and registering folks to vote. Some may recall that pre-pandemic I’d tell people that if they saw me out and about, or at a CB6 meeting, to ask me for a voter registration form if they needed one. Well, in the rare good sign of the times, the NY State Senate has passed a bill that will allow online voting registration in NYC. This doesn’t stop anyone from registering by mail, at the DMV or dropping that registration form at the Board of Elections , but what it does do is add one more way, faster than the other options, for people to have their voice heard and participate in democracy.

Our census has always at least attempted to count everyone living in our country, but now arbitrarily and by dictate our xenophobic head of state just decided to use the 2020 census to reduce future services for places like NYC. Aside from being illegal, it’s just plain wrong as the census doesn’t exist to count every person of certain types. It exists to count every person in the country. It now becomes even more important that we fill out the census and make sure to support the work of CB6’s own Jason Reischel and others to make every New Yorker Count, Speaking of filling out the census, in less than 10 minutes, y ou can do it here .  

Last but not least don’t forget that tomorrow, Thursday July 23rd, beginning at 7 PM, we are co-sponsoring a “ back to school” town hall with Councilmember Brad Lander. The town hall will feature leadership from the Department of Education, including Deputy Chancellor Adrienne Austin, Executive Superintendent Karen Watts, and District 15 Superintendent Anita Skop.

There are some other items you can check on below, but if you don’t, and this is where we part, enjoy the rest of your Wednesday.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201

item.title: Today, Tomorrow, Thursday
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: As previewed in newsletters over the past week, our Economic Development Committee met last night with a focus on businesses in our district during, and beyond, COVID. The keyword of the various presenters was "uncertainty".
item.content:encoded:
As previewed in newsletters over the past week, our Economic Development Committee met last night with a focus on businesses in our district during, and beyond, COVID. The keyword of the various presenters was "uncertainty". Too many businesses may well be failing - in the bar and restaurant sector, as colder weather arrives without a shift in circumstances. Theaters and wellness are already in deep trouble. The commercial real estate sector has been relatively stable due to warehousing/distribution; store lease prices have lowered but not substantially yet. Will people who have left the city return, and will those who work at home return to offices? It’s all uncertain.

Our new member, Natasha Amott, did a great job of running the Zoom, and a big thank you goes out to her. Also, another big thank you to all our guests including CEO of the Brooklyn Chamber of Commerce Randy Peers, James Dean Ellis of the North Flatbush BID , Mark Caserta of the Park Slope 5th Avenue BID , Ben Margolis of Southwest Brooklyn Industrial Development Corporation , Karen Narefsky of the Association for Neighborhood & Housing Development , as well as our very own, CB6 member and executive director of the Carroll Gardens Association , Vilma Heremia.

There was a consensus that there is a need for additional cash grants in the hardest-hit sectors and more clarity and consistency in government regulation, particularly concerning outdoor dining. However, it was also noted that outdoor dining does not work in all corridors or other parts of the district. The complex interrelationship of tenants, landlords, and tax revenue has not been resolved, and is made more difficult without bank and insurer participation. We also need a sufficient federal stimulus ASAP.

Again, please don’t forget that on Thursday, beginning at 7 PM, we are co-sponsoring a “back to school” town hall with Councilmember Brad Lander. The town hall will feature leadership from the Department of Education, including Deputy Chancellor Adrienne Austin, Executive Superintendent Karen Watts, and District 15 Superintendent Anita Skop.

There are some other items you can check on below, but if you don’t, and this is where we part, enjoy the rest of your Tuesday.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: Clarifications, Notifications, Phases
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well in the face of Covid-19 infection records that are being set across the country. Here in New York, even though we have the audacity to do testing, we've been keeping the curve nice and flat by keeping our…
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well in the face of Covid-19 infection records that are being set across the country. Here in New York, even though we have the audacity to do testing, we've been keeping the curve nice and flat by keeping our distance and covering our faces. As we close out phase 3 of our "reopening" this weekend, don't stop what's gotten us here, no matter how young, healthy or invincible you think you are.

Before recommending you check some of the items below my signature, I want to make a few points of clarification regarding announcements made by officials above me in the hierarchy of government as set forth in the city charter and state constitution.

First, our Governor said that there will no longer be walk-up bar service and that people can only order alcohol with food. If you're thinking, "well, not all bars have food," you should be ready for food items, such as chips that may cost as little as 5 cents a bag—to a required part of your order. Also, as there was some justified confusion over this, cocktails to-go will still be allowed . One opportunity to make this become a non-issue would be the passage of Assemblymember Carroll's bill, which would legalize open containers and drinking in public for the duration of the pandemic.

Second, also on the topic of drinking and eating outside the home, the Mayor announced that the Open Streets & Open Restaurants initiative would be extended through October 31st along with 40 more streets being added to this program . In our community, it includes Fifth Avenue from President Street to 3rd Street and, also, on 5th Avenue from 10th Street to 13th Street as organized by the Park Slope 5th Ave BID.

Speaking of the 5th Avenue BID, they, along with many other organizations, will be part of Monday night's Economic Development Committee meeting . Speaking of Monday, Alternate Side Parking regulations will also be resuming .

I'll once again try to clarify the cryptic announcements regarding the resumption of Alternate Side Parking(ASP) regulations. On a residential block with only 1 day listed on the ASP signs on that side of the Street, that's the day that side of the road will be swept, A/K/A NO CHANGES . However, if there are 2 or 3, ASP days listed for one side of the Street, it will ONLY be cleaned on the last day listed. So, for example, if the signs on one side of the block list "Tuesday and Friday" as ASP and the other side lists "Monday and Wednesday, "one side of the Street will be swept once on Wednesday and the other side on Friday. There are no changes to non -residential areas .

If anything changes on ASP or any of the other items, you'll hear from me. Stay safe and have a great weekend!

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Resuming Review
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I'll start by saying after yesterday's criticisms of those in their 20s for not taking the pandemic seriously enough, I was pleasantly surprised based on email responses, that we have several subscribers in that demographic. Even at 35, I…
item.content:encoded:
I'll start by saying after yesterday's criticisms of those in their 20s for not taking the pandemic seriously enough, I was pleasantly surprised based on email responses, that we have several subscribers in that demographic. Even at 35, I feel prematurely old complaining about "kids these days," however I think it's justified when it helps do all we can to fight this virus, but I digress.

As some of you may have noticed, the Mayor announced, the Uniform Land Use Review Process (ULURP) is resuming , and the City Planning Commission will start holding online hearings beginning in August.

When ULURP's were initially put on hold back in March, we weren't reviewing any certified applications. However, the Gowanus rezoning looms at some point in the future. We've made clear that the Department of City Planning(DCP) should let us know what their plans are ASAP, along with lots of stuff you can read about here .

The rezoning was in the news as recently as yesterday with the Gowanus Neighborhood Coalition for Justice (GNCJ) reiterating their stance in City-limits. At the same time, you may recall that a few weeks back, there were dueling letters of support and opposition.

I haven't been given any sort of indication of a timeline from City Hall or DCP. However, if the rezoning is certified, we'll do everything we can to ensure as much input as possible. There are two points I'd like to clarify. First, finding my cell phone number and cursing me out, while at times funny, doesn't help advance your point of view, and, no matter what your perspective, please don't assume I disagree with you or that everyone else agrees with you. Let the process and any legal actions play out.

Anyway, I'll leave you for now, but suggest you read on passed my signature and if you go outside, keep your distance and cover your face (not either/or).

Have a good Thursday!

Related tools

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Kids these days
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: COVID numbers for NYC look “okay” for now, but there is a troubling detail buried within them concerning the infection rate for people in their twenties , which has nearly doubled in the last month. Nobody is invincible, and young people…
item.content:encoded:
COVID numbers for NYC look “okay” for now, but there is a troubling detail buried within them concerning the infection rate for people in their twenties , which has nearly doubled in the last month. Nobody is invincible, and young people can be a spearhead for a COVID-19, spike. Regardless of demographics, protect everyone else. I don’t know if many people under 30 read my emails, and those that do are probably among the most responsible, but please keep your distance & cover your face. Not just in the “my mask protects you” way but as an acknowledgment of the reality that the virus doesn’t discriminate, and nobody wants to go back into lockdown as have other states, including California .

In this fight, actions can have far-reaching consequences; for example, in New York State, had we “paused” one week earlier, based on a study from Columbia University,  17 thousand fewer people would have died. 

I don’t have much else to say aside from that reminder to stay vigilant in this fight. Take some solace in the efforts, encouraging signs of eventually having a vaccine and check out the items below my signature, which include next week 's CB6 EWCDH meeting and the back to school town-hall we’re sponsoring.

Enjoy the rest of your Wednesday, even if there’s one for you, nineteen for me.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Summer, Schools, Safely
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well on this warm summer Tuesday as we approach the much delayed Tax Day , which is tomorrow, July 15th. Not the most anxiously awaited part of the reopening.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well on this warm summer Tuesday as we approach the much delayed Tax Day , which is tomorrow, July 15th. Not the most anxiously awaited part of the reopening.

I’ll keep it brief but a few things I should highlight as we continue to do the work (face covered/distance) to keep the curve sufficiently flat and allow us to continue to progress in our phased reopening.

There’s some exciting virtual and in-person stuff such as Councilmember Lander’s Heat/Cool Green Rowhouse Webinar and the Cobble Hill Association’s “Stoopfest” and weaving with the Old Stone House.

Looking ahead to next week, I’d like to highlight 2 CB6 related events.

First, on Monday, July 20th at 6:30 PM, our Economic Waterfront Community Development and Housing (EWCDH) Committee will have a zoom meeting which will feature the Brooklyn Chamber of Commerce’s CEO Randy Peers, as well as, the Southwest Brooklyn Industrial Development Corporation’s Ben Margolis and Mark Caserta of the Park Slope 5th Avenue Business Improvement District. If you’d like to attend register here.

Second, on Thursday, July 23rd, beginning at 7:00 PM, we are co-sponsoring a Back-to-School Townhall with Councilmember Brad Lander. The Department of Education's' Deputy Chancellor Adrienne Austin, Executive Superintendent Karen Watts, and District 15 Superintendent Anita Skop will be available to answer questions from parents about scheduling logistics, child care, support for social and emotional well-being, and more. Just like the EWCDH meeting, you should register in advance by clicking here.

As always, I’d recommend checking out the items below, including Assemblymember Simon's summer reading challenge . No matter what you choose to do. I hope you do it safely and that you enjoy the rest of your Tuesday.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Sites, Stats, Starts
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well as we kick off the second week of Phase 3 after a jazz parade made an appearance in our district over the weekend. New York's Covid-19 statistics continue to show close to 1 percent infection rates and…
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well as we kick off the second week of Phase 3 after a jazz parade made an appearance in our district over the weekend. New York's Covid-19 statistics continue to show close to 1 percent infection rates and under ten deaths a day( no deaths in NYC Saturday ), although every death is still is a tragedy. The nation's statistics, on the other hand, especially in places that reopened early, such as Florida, set new records . So while, for those that get the reference, I sound like a broken record and to others just plain old repetitive, keep your distance and mask on.

I'll be brief before urging you to check out the items below. First Alternate Side Parking Is suspended until Sunday, July 19th. Also, please note that work on the BQE has been rescheduled to start today, July 13th , while work on the Union Street Bridge has been suspended until July 16th .

Keep scrolling for more information that may interest you. Whether you scroll or not, sit outside at a restaurant, or anything else we haven't been able to do, in case you haven't heard, keep your distance, with your face covered so you can enjoy the rest of the day and many more.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Testing, Jamming, Canceling, Schooling
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: The national record number of Covid-19 infections across the country reinforces that our rigorous practice of social distancing and face covering is working and that we need to keep doing it: no weekend rule suspensions or anything like…
item.content:encoded:
The national record number of Covid-19 infections across the country reinforces that our rigorous practice of social distancing and face covering is working and that we need to keep doing it: no weekend rule suspensions or anything like that.

Speaking of suspensions, the City has canceled all large permitted events (not block parties) through September 30th while Alternate Side Parking regulations are back in effect starting this coming Monday, July 13th and if that were to change I'd send out a notice immediately. Also, as the specifics of the, not quite suspended, 2020/2021 school year are determined, I've been in discussions with District 15's leadership. I'd like to note ho helpful D15 has been throughout the pandemic. I will pass along

information and clarifications on this matter as it is received.

Over the weekend, there are things to do aside from waiting for the next newsletter. You can, for example, read this piece on street uses, go to a boathouse jam , check out open streets and open restaurants , keep reading this email, or anything else you can do safely. Keep in mind the safer we all are, the faster we’ll get to phase 4 of our reopening, and some semblance of normalcy or, as Dr. Fauci says, normality.

No matter what you choose to do, in case you missed the point: stay safe,wear a mask, and have a good weekend.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Returning, Learning,Cooling
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: As always, I hope this email finds you well on this 9th day of the 7th month of the year of the pandemic.
item.content:encoded:
As always, I hope this email finds you well on this 9th day of the 7th month of the year of the pandemic. 

During this time of COVID-19, nothing is normal, or least not the old normal, and some things happen, at least in my own experience, that makes you say, “wow, this is different.” A prime example is the Mayor’s Announcement that public schools would still not fully reopen in September . Classroom attendance will instead be limited to only one to three days a week to continue curbing the coronavirus outbreak. 

Our city’s public school system has 1.1 million students, making it the largest in the nation, so the impact of this is not a small matter, and there is still a lot to determine how this will be implemented. As I find out more, you will too. I’ve already spoken with District 15 superintendent, and a great friend to CB6, Anita Skop. Then Superintendent informed me that she’d present to CB6 once there is more information and clarity are surrounding what the upcoming school year will look like. 

Until then, keep reading these newsletters as I’ll continue to share updates on this and plenty of other important matters. Some of those matters, including guidance for reopening restaurants and “ Cool ” streets, can be found below my email signature, so read on and enjoy the rest of your Thursday. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

The 3rd day of the 3rd phase sounds like a twilight zone episode, yet it is our reality this Wednesday, July 8th, 2020.

Today is NYC’s “ Day of Action ” for all New Yorkers to get tested for COVID-19 . Even if you do not have symptoms, getting tested can save others' lives, and it’s free! Find a location here or by clicking the flyers found further on down the metaphorical road that is this email. Anyway, I’m not going to say much and delay you possibly getting a test so I’ll leave you now.

Whether you take my advice or not, enjoy the rest of this third day of the third phase.

item.title: The Long Count & More
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Forgive a brief rant from a political junkie, but there was a primary election last week, and we may still be weeks away from knowing the winner in many races here in our community, and across the borough, and city. While it’s more…
item.content:encoded:
Forgive a brief rant from a political junkie, but there was a primary election last week, and we may still be weeks away from knowing the winner in many races here in our community, and across the borough, and city. While it’s more important to achieve an accurate count than a fast one, this delay calls out for election reforms such as those outlined by Congresswoman Velázquez in her letter to the New York City Board of Elections. We can’t change the past, but this is an opportunity to improve the future. We certainly shouldn’t hesitate to reform a government agency that cites a “ shortage of envelopes “ as a reason to oppose voting by mail.

Regardless of your thoughts on such matters, I’d recommend checking out the items below my signature, including a GCC plant sale, a democratic event at The Old Stone House and more. Continuing with the theme of my political addiction, if you can, I’d recommend streaming , ”Hamilton.” History wrapped in rap.

Enough of my theatrical thoughts, keep your distance, wear a mask, and enjoy the rest of your Tuesday.

Related tools

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: Two, three, eventually four Save this email as a link
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well after the holiday weekend as we kick off “ Phase 3 ” of the reopening.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well after the holiday weekend as we kick off “ Phase 3 ” of the reopening. 

Phase 3 means you can get a tattoo, get a manicure, play some basketball, and follow it up with a massage. This is all going at the pace and schedule that was outlined but with one big exception, and that is, we still won't have indoor dining. For that reason, the city is moving forward with plans to expand outdoor dining options with more “Open Streets” for restaurants. As of now, there are open streets for restaurants in our district along with other blocks in Red Hook, and more can be applied for here . Even where they aren’t “open” the outdoor has received rave reviews . 

No matter the food or where it’s eaten, we have to keep up the discipline that allowed us to flatten the Covid-19 curve to a remarkable degree . If we don’t keep it up, there will be a spike , and we will risk shutting down/ hitting “ pause ” again.

On a positive note, New York City has not missed a benchmark since beginning its reopening in early June. If that trend holds, the city may be cleared for phase four in mid-July, which includes “Low risk" activities such as going to museums, zoos, botanical gardens, pro sporting events taking place without live spectators, and something on the minds of parents, teachers, and students, schools opening. 

As I find out more about these and other matters through all phases, I’ll share it. For now, I’d say keep scrolling down and enjoy the rest of your Monday.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Independence Day Weekend
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: We at Brooklyn Community Board 6 wish you all the best as we head into Independence Day weekend. These are tough times across our nation, but we've faced troubled times before, and we overcame them. W
item.content:encoded:
We at Brooklyn Community Board 6 wish you all the best as we head into Independence Day weekend.

These are tough times across our nation, but we've faced troubled times before, and we overcame them. We created an aspirational nation that kept hope alive during a civil war and beat back tyranny in two world wars. We persevered through pandemic and depression. We are again called upon in the name of justice and freedom to be our best selves even as we struggle through the ravages of disease and economic collapse. We must show the fortitude to move forward as a country and in our community, and we have no doubt we will.

So enjoy this holiday weekend at a safe distance, and while you may disagree with what someone says or believes, not only do they have the right to do it, criticism of a system should not be confused for hate or disrespect. It's why James Baldwin said , when asked about his criticism of this country, born out of a declaration 244 years ago , 'I love America more than any other country in the world and, exactly for this reason, I insist on the right to criticize her perpetually".

Resources, Reminders, Items of Interest

Businesses Resources & Listings

item.title: Collapse, Suspension, Streets & Loss
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I’ll start with news of the building collapse at 348 Court Street, best known as the location of Body Elite Gym. I’ve been in contact with Councilmember Lander, Inspector O’Malley, and the Office of Emergency Management on the matter.
item.content:encoded:
I’ll start with news of the building collapse at 348 Court Street, best known as the location of Body Elite Gym. I’ve been in contact with Councilmember Lander, Inspector O’Malley, and the Office of Emergency Management on the matter. The cause is still being investigated, but thankfully nobody, as of yet, has been injured or displaced. This collapsed building had been issued a stop-work order three weeks ago. As I receive more information, I’ll be sure to share it with you and please note the road closures happening in the area.

Speaking of information to share, next Monday, July 6th, begins “ Phase 3 ” of our reopening. Unlike Phase 2, where a lot of businesses returned, the only category set to return under Phase 3 is personal care. Unfortunately, due to the resurgence of COVID-19 across the country, attributed in large part to indoor dining, indoor dining has been indefinitely delayed. Phase 3 will also see a host of recreational activities such as basketball and tennis being permitted once again. But no matter what you do, please keep your distance and cover your face as the COVID-19 crisis is very much still happening no matter how much some of us want to wish it away.

Sadly, we have a reminder of just how current this crisis  is, as we lost former Assemblymember Joe Ferris to COVID-19 just over a week ago. I didn’t know him, but many people I know and respect always spoke of him as a significant force for good in the government. Among those paying tribute are his  Assembly successors Jim Brennan and now, Robert Carroll, as well as great reformers in neighboring districts such as Mike Pesce, Jo Anne Simon, and my old boss Joan Millman. We offer the most profound condolences to the Ferris family.

Lastly, enjoy the rest of your day, and if you don’t hear from me, have a good and safe 4th of July.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Un
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well as we kick off July and the city’s fiscal year. I’d say “Happy Fiscal New Year” if the budget’s themes were anything more than painful cuts and shifts that, in some cases, were just cosmetic reforms.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well as we kick off July and the city’s fiscal year. I’d say “Happy Fiscal New Year” if the budget’s themes were anything more than painful cuts and shifts that, in some cases, were just cosmetic reforms.

However, even within such a bad budget , there are bright spots such as reallocating close to 600 million dollars into the NYCHA and summer youth programming funding for which we at Community Board 6 have repeatedly advocated as paramount needs for our community.

Even though the COVID curve has flattened here, we'll still need significant assistance from either or both the federal and state governments in your order to avoid worse cuts that are looming down the road. Our budget and economy don’t exist in a vacuum, and for the fourth time in a week, the United States posted new single-day Covid-19 case records. So let that serve as a reminder to cover your face and keep a safe distance.

At this point, I wish the City never announced any changes to Alternate Side Parking(ASP) . Based on anecdotal reports I'm getting, it’s creating more confusion than relief. So I’ll try to clarify again - on a residential block with only 1 day listed on the ASP signs on that side of the street that’s the day that side of the road will be swept, AKA NO CHANGES. However, if there are 2 or 3, ASP days listed for one side of the street, it will ONLY be cleaned on the last day listed. So, for example, if the signs on one side of the block list “Tuesday and Friday” as ASP and the other side lists “Monday and Wednesday, “ the street will be swept once on Wednesday and once on Friday. There are no changes to non -residential areas. I’ve fielded quite a few inquiries on this, but if you have any questions about ASP, I’ll get the answer for you ASAP.

Just like the other weekdays, today will be much better if you check out the items of interest further down this email.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

So, for example, if the signs on one side of the block list “Tuesday and Friday” as ASP and the other side lists “Monday and Wednesday, “ the street will be swept once on Wednesday and once on Friday. There are no changes to non -residential areas. I’ve fielded quite a few inquiries on this, but if you have any questions about ASP, I’ll get the answer for you ASAP.

Just like the other weekdays, today will be much better if you check out the items of interest further down this email.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: Virtually, Literally
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well during the earth’s final rotation of June and the end of New York City’s fiscal year.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well during the earth’s final rotation of June and the end of New York City’s fiscal year.

Tomorrow starts FY 2021 as New York City government is slated to finalize and pass the budget later today. Much like FY 2020, it will include minimal good news and a considerable sleight of hand. It may even get worse as we get further into the year. Sorry that this seems generally negative, but one silver lining is that some of the youth funding, which we had pushed f or, has been restored . Our advocacy predated its inclusion as a social movement goal , and we are glad it gathered momentum for inclusion. It demonstrates that being on the ground and listening community has enduring value to the city that should be preserved in the budgeting process.

I’ll, of course, share more information as I receive it. Still, I wanted to remind you to have a heads up for authorized fireworks happening this evening and throughout the week to celebrate Independence Day. The purpose of having a week-long, stealthy “celebration,” is to avoid large gatherings while acknowledging the holiday. Follow the rules, and next year we can have an old fashioned good time.

Speaking of resources, I know the Alternate Side Parking changes are, at best, slightly confusing The bottom line is that if you are parked on a residential block that has signs indicating ASP occurring once a week on each side, NOTHING CHANGES . If you have further questions, I will, of course, do what I can to find out the answers as simply & quickly as possible.

Enjoy the rest of your day, see you next month, and I’d recommend checking out the items below. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well after a weekend that saw the return of outdoor dining and the 50th anniversary of the Pride March and the 51st anniversary of the Stonewall Riots. 

Please be aware that tonight begins the five day series of 5-minute fireworks which is, ostensibly, replacing July 4th fireworks with these smaller displays. They’ll take place at undisclosed locations to prevent crowds from gathering and, thus, risk spreading COVID-19. Im not in the mood for fireworks, but if we're going to have fireworks, it's best to do so in a way that prevents the kind of infection spikes that are setting new records every day across our country and across the globe.

For preventive measures, and in honor of sticking with what’s working, no matter what you do, cover your face, keep your distance and enjoy the rest of this final Monday of June.

I’d close by mentioning that today will be much better if you check out the items of interest further down this email.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.description: I hope this email finds you well as we transition seamlessly from remote learning and teaching on the last day of school for New York City's public school to stay/vacation time. Congrats to EVERYONE for getting through it.
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well as we transition seamlessly from remote learning and teaching on the last day of school for New York City's public school to stay/vacation time. Congrats to EVERYONE for getting through it. While school's out for summer, it isn't out forever, and hopefully, everyone can return to classrooms safely and sooner than later. An especially big congratulations to everyone who is graduating - if nothing else, when graduating in 2020, you'll never have to wonder if your experience was unique to all that have donned a cap and gown .

As a city we're heading to the weekend and on pace to be in " Phase 3 " of "reopening" on Monday, July 6th. That would mean, among other things, a significant expansion of our recreational resources (basketball, TENNIS, etc.), so please keep your distance and cover your face. Not doing so could lead to remaining in phase 2 or worse. I'm not saying this on a wing and a prayer. I'm saying it because when people don't take these precautions seriously, Covid-19 cases spike , and when they do, even with densely attended protests , the spread is slowed.

Anyway, have a good weekend, stay safe, check out the items below, including art , acoustic jams , ASP changes , and more.

Best,

item.title: Alternate Explanation , Beaches & More
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Most results from Tuesday's election are still being determined as the record-setting number of people that voted by mail together with the Board of Elections being understaffed and underfunded combined with standard levels of incompetence…
item.content:encoded:
Most results from Tuesday's election are still being determined as the record-setting number of people that voted by mail together with the Board of Elections being understaffed and underfunded combined with standard levels of incompetence means we won't have official results until next week. However, Congresswoman Nydia Velasquez has already been declared the winner in her race, and we are fortunate to have her representing many CB6 communities on Capitol Hill.

I have 2 more items, after which I'd recommend scrolling past my email signature to check out other notices.

First, NYC beaches will open on July 1st

Secondly, yesterday's announcement that starting next week Alternate Side Parking was shifting to once a week , as do all things parking related, received a lot of responses and questions. The general theme of the questions was, 'does this mean only one side of my block gets cleaned?" The answer is "no."  This change only matters for streets where there are multiple ASP days per side. For example, if one side of your block has street sweeping on Monday and the other side has it on Thursday, Cars on the Monday side move on Monday, cars on the Thursday side move on Thursday. So if you move from side to side, you must move on both days. That is the extended version of saying your block will see no change .

Keep reading to be fully informed and, either way, safely enjoy the rest of your Thursday.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Al's Advice, Alternate Side & More
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I won't offer any premature congratulations to anyone regarding yesterday's primary election as a record number of mail-in ballots are to be counted. Of course, as seems to be the case every time we try to have an election, the Board of…
item.content:encoded:
I won't offer any premature congratulations to anyone regarding yesterday's primary election as a record number of mail-in ballots are to be counted. Of course, as seems to be the case every time we try to have an election, the Board of Election definitively lost . I heard from many constituents about problems and inconsistencies in policies across the district.

Such a pattern deserves to be fixed through systemic reforms, and also, let's face it, a state that will allocate the proper amounts of resources to run elections. This is never good but especially problematic at a time when we need safety to be paramount and have a presidential election this year, yesterday's problems aren't going to go away unless we find a way because general elections have far higher turnout and ultimate consequences.

For all my negativity, while personally pleased with some results so far, I take solace and look to a former New York Governor, Al Smith , who said All "the ills of democracy can be cured by more democracy."

Related tools

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

item.title: Juneteenth, Phase 2, The Weekend
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: Juneteenth a/k/a June 19th marks 155 years since the last proclamation of the end of slavery. It, of course, happens amid a national uprising against police violence and systemic racism unlike any I’ve seen in my admittedly not so long…
item.content:encoded:
Juneteenth a/k/a June 19th marks 155 years since the last proclamation of the end of slavery. It, of course, happens amid a national uprising against police violence and systemic racism unlike any I’ve seen in my admittedly not so long lifetime. Millions are likely to be observing, what by next year will be, a city and state holiday, for the first time.

It’s a day and an issue that requires many of us, especially folks such as myself, to think about inherent advantages and biases in ourselves and structures we have supported and from which we have benefited. That can mean something as simple as ignoring the amount of funding certain parts of government receive while others get cut or eliminated. It also means not only listening to what people are saying but making changes based on alternate experiences

Our problems are social and human creations and, therefore, can be fixed by humans. It won’t be easy to reassess, but it will be worth it. It can start with something as simple as heeding our call to restore funding for the Summer Youth Employment Program.

I’ve cited Samuel Beckett's "Worstward Ho" before, but it still feels like apt advice so here it is again:

"All of old. Nothing else ever. Ever tried. Ever failed. No matter. Try again. Fail again. Fail better."

Since giving up is not an option, it is all we can do.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well on this cloudy Thursday. So, we're headed to phase 2 on Monday, so what does that mean?

It means we took a small step out of the woods, and we may eat outside, go to bars and restaurants with outdoor dining, get haircuts, return to offices, engage in retail shopping and have fun at playgrounds. The permanence of this better life is dependent on following safety protocols, such as distancing and masking, that will help keep us on a path towards phase 3 and 4. As I’ve noted, I can’t wait to get a haircut, but if that’s the worst part of my pandemic experience, I’ll consider myself very lucky. Businesses with questions about the process can call the city’s hotline at 1-888-SBS-4NYC.

Lastly, as usual, I’d suggest checking out the items below, including coverage of Gowanus related letters, and enjoy the rest of your day.

item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well as we start week 2 of Phase 1 while hoping that one week from today, we'll start phase 2 . If that were to happen it would be a relief for those among us who have been deprived of a haircut since before Saint Patrick's Day and appear to be feral. Of course, haircuts and restaurants, are a matter of comfort and are by no means guaranteed. We are still vigilantly tracking COVID-19 infections and renewal of lockdown orders is a possibility. item.title: Thursday, June 11, 2020
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: COVID-19 cases drop here , spike there , and persistent and pernicious symbols of treason fall across the land. I’m not confusing statues and symbols to be anywhere near as important as policy changes, but they are still welcome.
item.content:encoded:
COVID-19 cases drop here , spike there , and persistent and pernicious symbols of treason fall across the land. I’m not confusing statues and symbols to be anywhere near as important as policy changes, but they are still welcome. A collective statement of positive civic values and rejection of a Confederate identity promoting racial supremacy is long overdue. Doubly so when one considers the lack of contrasting symbols reminding us of the horrors of the slavery that the Confederacy wanted to maintain. NASCAR is not my thing, but I do care that this significant cultural institution finally decouples from an emblem of slavery, which has been celebrated under the guise of ”culture.”

Anyway, well above the Mason-Dixon line, but below my email signature, there are items of interest that I’d recommend checking out. If not, no problem, and enjoy the rest of your day.

Best,

item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you well as we start phase 1 of the “reopening .” It’s important to not let up on social distancing and covering our faces, as letting up could lead to more tragedies and prevent us from getting to the next phase.…
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you well as we start phase 1 of the “reopening .” It’s important to not let up on social distancing and covering our faces, as letting up could lead to more tragedies and prevent us from getting to the next phase. I’d like to dine at a restaurant and get my haircut (I have already had some constructive criticism my current look) sometime soon. Due to awkward phrasing in the previous sentence, I want to make clear; I will get my haircut at a barbershop, not at a restaurant. Of course, hair care and dining plans pale in significance with the multipronged crisis we’re facing.

It was great to see our community engage in a peaceful protest starting in Red Hook yesterday. Hopefully, it will continue to remind us that we have the means to be heard and the power to change things. Speaking of change, and coincidentally Red Hook, Assemblymember Ortiz’s Bill making it a hate crime when 911 callers make false accusations based on race, gender or religion is likely to be among many upcoming reforms. 

Of course, we’ll see what happens in these crazy times of ours. The items below my email signature may contain some information that helps you navigate by answering a question or 2. I’m biased in favor of you reading them, but no matter what you decide, enjoy the rest of your day.

item.title: Phasing under Curfew
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: As always, I hope this email finds you well as we head into, hopefully, the only curfewed weekend of our adult lives and start the phased " reopening " on Monday.
item.content:encoded:
As always, I hope this email finds you well as we head into, hopefully, the only curfewed weekend of our adult lives and start the phased " reopening " on Monday.

No matter how or when we "reopen" unless there are policies in place to keep us safe while also stimulating the economy and minimizing current economic pain, the pain will become a persistent fact of life. While the city is looking at options to help the economy, the state has even more options. Still, the Federal Government has the most, and without help from the Federal Government, something such as today's encouraging jobs report will be fleeting and compound the crisis we face in the future.

As discussed earlier in the week, the system we see breaking down is a social system; thus, human, and therefore, with a lot of hard work from a lot of people, can be fixed by people. You could start by getting a ballot for our June 23rd primary, but civic participation needs to become a habit passed the pandemic( you’re already reading a community board newsletter). It's not going be easy, but in whatever formal and creative roles I have, I will do my best to bind us to each other.

Anyway, just like the world before COVID and curfews, there is some useful information below the email signature. Stay safe, enjoy the weekend and speak to you Monday.

item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I don’t have any philosophical explorations today. In the absence of such musings, let me remind you that our citywide curfew remains in place until, coincidentally, we begin the first phase of the “reopening” on Monday.
item.content:encoded:
I don’t have any philosophical explorations today. In the absence of such musings, let me remind you that our citywide curfew remains in place until, coincidentally, we begin the first phase of the “reopening” on Monday. This means construction, manufacturing, wholesalers, and curbside retail stores are permitted to operate with safety measures in place. I can’t wait for “ Phase 2 ” when restaurants may have an outdoor dining service. That could happen as soon as June 22nd , so let’s continue to cover our faces while outside, so we avoid any setbacks. Another, perhaps less welcome, part of “phase one” is the return of Alternate Side Parking regulations. 

My opening remarks are brief, but as always, there are numerous items of interest and use below my email signature. Enjoy the rest of your day and stay safe. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager

I don't know if it's due to COVID-19, the content or curfew paired with a compulsion to send a newsletter every weekday, but whatever the reason is, I'd like to say "thank you" for the tremendous response it has received, especially the last two days . Anyone who enjoys riffing on Rousseau is a friend of mine.

Again, we're asked to be inside before 8 PM and every day until Monday, June 8th. June 8tth is also, Ironically, and fittingly, the day we begin phase one of " reopening " from the COVID-19 stay at home order. Remember when you come home from protests or when we officially reopen be mindful of others who may be vulnerable.

 The MTA has announced that the ' " reopenin g " will be the return of 'regular service." I used quotes for "regular service'' because it is what the MTA said but, since it won't include 24 service , it's not quite accurate. I'm not a linguist or a lawyer, but I don't see how anything can be characterized as returning to "regular" while ignoring mentioning something that hadn't stopped for over a century .

Anyway, just like regular weekdays, and almost always before 8 PM, there are some useful items below my email signature. Stay safe and enjoy the rest of the day as much as you can.

item.title: Curfews & Contracts
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I'd like to start by thanking everyone who reached out after yesterday's newsletter. I never knew Samuel Beckett would resonate so strongly.
item.content:encoded:
I'd like to start by thanking everyone who reached out after yesterday's newsletter. I never knew Samuel Beckett would resonate so strongly. Anyway, since I turned 18, I hadn't thought of a curfew applying to me or any of my peers. Yet, here we are. 

A city of over 8 million must be hunkered down before 8 pm tonight until 5 am until Sunday June 7th.

Whether one thinks it is necessary or not, it is unquestionably a bad sign. It recalls dark periods of history. It hasn't happened since 1943 , and again highlights a system that, for millions of people, was broken long before any of us heard of the Coronavirus. This is particularly troubling as physical laws are out of our control. So if one is stranded on a desert island, no amount of faith or want can make saltwater quench your thirst; paper currency cannot be ingested as sustenance, nor can anyone flap their arms and fly. 

The social contract, and all that it entails, is only as binding as we, collectively, make it. It's how we determine what rights people have, what laws are, and how we express our values. There are, of course, lots of things that go into this complex unwritten contract. It differs across the world based on norms, values and customs in countries, states, cities, or any other designation of governing body. It can mean that a single dollar is enough to buy a house, or it can mean that everyone gets healthcare or even why words mean what they mean.

No matter the example for a social system/contract to be sustainable, it requires some degree of consent from the governed. When it comes to governing, I don't mean being necessarily supportive of a policy or action in society. Consent can be achieved through passive means and even collective ignorance, through fear and intimidation, or through a simple analysis of inadequate resources. Unlike physical laws, usually after persistent and wide-scale failings, these social, and therefore human, systems break down. 

At 8 pm, we will witness the results of a system breaking down, and It's not easy to fathom. I won't pretend to be an optimist, but I take some solace in that that you, I, and anyone reading this are human and part of an evolving social contract. Therefore, we have the collective resources (not just those reading) to change the system. It's not going be easy, but in whatever formal and creative roles I have I will do my best to bind us to each other.

It's the only option we have, even if that means simply failing better until we try again.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.title: Worstward
item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: These newsletters are more musical comedy and drama then Shakespearian, but I enjoy getting them out, and anyone who knows me knows I rarely stop speaking but I'm having a tough time finding any words today. We're living through what seems…
item.content:encoded:
These newsletters are more musical comedy and drama then Shakespearian, but I enjoy getting them out, and anyone who knows me knows I rarely stop speaking but I'm having a tough time finding any words today. We're living through what seems to be a snowballing health, economic, safety, and justice crisis that feels like it is turning into an avalanche.

I join those who have related Samuel Beckett's "Worstward Ho" to our current situation.

﻿

To reinforce its resonance, I say:

"All of old. Nothing else ever. Ever tried. Ever failed. No matter. Try again. Fail again. Fail better."

Since giving up is not an option, it is all we can do. 

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org

item.dc:creator: Mike Racioppo
item.description: I hope this email finds you as well as can be as we head into the final days of May and plan to start " reopening " on June 8 th . No matter what you're paying attention to, unless you're a billionaire , I'd find it hard to see a landscape…
item.content:encoded:
I hope this email finds you as well as can be as we head into the final days of May and plan to start " reopening " on June 8 th . No matter what you're paying attention to, unless you're a billionaire , I'd find it hard to see a landscape that is any better than sobering to horrifying .

We have to get through it, and I am confident we will. I could do with fewer advertisements and articles suggesting people leave the city. I've don't know if I've ever been to Hackensack but, just like Bobby Short sang , if I ended up there, I'd take the next train back.

As is the case Monday through Friday, some items below my email signature could be put to good use. Whether you check them out or not, I hope you have a good weekend, stay safe, and keep covering your face.

Best,
Mike Racioppo, District Manager
Brooklyn Community Board 6 · 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Mike@bkcb6.org
